Nuclear Disarmament—Treaty on the Non-proliferation of Nuclear Weapons
Review Conference

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: I seek the leave of the House to move
without notice and without debate a motion relating to the forthcoming Nuclear Non-
proliferation Treaty Review Conference, asking the nuclear States to meet their
commitments.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will just put the leave. Leave is sought. Is there any objection to
that course of action being followed? The Hon Phil Goff.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: I move, That this House urge nuclear weapons States at this
year’s Nuclear Non- proliferation Treaty Review Conferenc e in New York in April to
fulfil their side of the bargain they struck 45 years ago in signing a treaty to eliminate
their nuclear weapons in exchange for other nations not prolifer ating nuclear weapons,
and call on them to now act to honour their unequivoc al undertaking to disarm under
Article 6 of the treaty.
Motion agreed to.

Roading, Northland—Bridges Upgrade
1. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader —NZ First) to the Prime Minister: Does
he stand by all his statements regarding the Northland by-election?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, in the context they were given.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Does he stand by his statement regarding the 10 one -lane
bridges that “these bridges need upgrading and they will be.”; if so, how does he explain
a massive variation in costings of between $32 million and $69 million?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: In answer to the first part of the question, yes; in answer to the
second part of the question, not all the work has been done to be absolutely sure of what
the final costs will be. That is standard whenever we do procurement around new
infrastructure like roading.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Whose idea was it to double lane the 10 bridges, and on
what date was he informed that the announcement would be made?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: In answer to the first part of the question, Cabinet.
2786 Oral Questions  1 Apr 2015

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Well, how does he square that answer with the Northland
National Party candidate’s statement that it was his idea? Who is not telling the truth
here?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The question has been asked.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member did not ask me where the idea originated from.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I know that you study the Hansard
of questions and answers and I know that you are fully awa re that these questions were
asked on 10 March and on 17 March, and that the Ministers and Cabinet, particularly
the Minister of Transport, have had all that time to get these answers right and to be
able to answer them truthfully in the House. I ask that you require them to do that.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am not sure that is a point of order, but if the member
thinks that an answer has been given in this House that is incorrect, there is an
appropriate way to deal with that, and it is not via a point of order.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. But surely it would be far cheaper
for the taxpayer if we do not go through—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will resume his seat. That is certainly not a
clarification and it is not a point of order.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Is he in favour of the “Darby and Joan” Bridge being
double-laned, considering that it would require cutting down two landmark, protected
native kauri trees, and that very low numbers of vehicles actually use the bridge —often
just to see those kauri trees?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am advised that the member is incorrect in the assumptions
he made in his question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. What has happened
here is that the Prime Minister has got up and challenged the very veracity of the
question, which simply was that it is a landmark bridge—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is a point of order.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: —and it got an environmental award because it harmonises
with the two kauri trees, and he says I am incorrect with my assumptions.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Point of order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I do not need assistance from the member. The member asked a
question. The Prime Minister disputed the facts that are in that question. That is the
right of the Prime Minister. The way forward is supplementary questions.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I have ruled on this matter. I am not putting up with a repetition
of yesterday where my points —[Interruption] Would the member sit down.
[Interruption] Order! I am very tempted t o be asking the member to leave. The member
can continue asking his supplementary questions if he has some left, but I have ruled
that the question that was asked has been addressed.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: When I said that somebody w as in favour of the “Darby
and Joan” Bridge being double-laned and that it would end the landmark, historical, and
environmental award given to this bridge because of the kauri trees that have to be cut
down, which one of those assumptions was wrong?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: That was not the question the member asked me.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I have studied the
Westminster system all around the world, and I have never seen—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! A point of order has been called. I will
listen to it and I expect to listen to it in silence. Would the member quickly get to his
point of order.
1 Apr 2015 Oral Questions  2787

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: My point of order is that I am asking the Prime Minister to
outline what assumptions he says we have got wrong in our questions on this matter.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I think the problem here is that had Mr Peters been able to
table a full design specification for the renewed “Darby and Joan” Bridge, he might be
able to make the assertions he has, but he cannot and he does not need to make these
assertions until that is the case.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I am not sure that helps us forward in this case. The Rt Hon
Winston Peters has now been—

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Point of order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I am on my feet. He has repeated now a question that is not the
question he asked and that is the difficulty. The question was a very long -winded
question. The Prime Minister has addressed that question—I accept not to the member’s
satisfaction. [Interruption] Order! The way forward is further supplementary questions.
It is not to then question the answer that has been given.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Wins ton Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I asked this question
No. 4 in one way and the answer was that I got the assumptions wrong. I asked the
question in a different way—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Again, I have dealt  with this. Sit down. The member asked
the question. The Prime Minister addressed the question— I have said, to my
satisfaction; I accept it is not to the member’s satisfaction. The way forward is further
supplementary questions.

items.speaker: Rt H on Winston Peters
items.text: Is he in favour of the “Darby and Joan” Bridge being
double-laned, considering that it would require cutting down two landmark, protected
native kauri trees, and that very low numbers of vehicles actually use the bridge —often
just to see those trees?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: In answer to the first part of the question, yes. In answer to the
second part of the question, the member is wrong. The trees will not be cut down.
Economy—Impact on Families
2. ALASTAIR SCOTT (National—Wairarapa) to the Minister of Finance: What
reports has he received showing how the performance of the New Zealand economy is
translating into benefits for New Zealand families?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yesterday ANZ released its
economic outlook report for March. It indicated that the momentum of last year’s
economic growth is likely to continue into this year , and it expects 3 percent growth for
this year. It points out that there are risks to the New Zealand economy related to low
energy and low commodity prices, but it expects job growth, wage growth, and
continued low interest rates, which for households me ans job security, moderate wage
increases, and a greater ability to repay debt rather than pay higher interest rates.

items.speaker: Alastair Scott
items.text: What measures come into effect today that will directly benefit New
Zealand families?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The prospect of sustainable economic growth means that the
Government is able to act to support families. So from 1 April paid parental leave will
increase by 2 weeks to 16 weeks, and by another 2 weeks on 1 April next year. The
parental tax credit will rise from $150 a week to $220, and the entitlement will increase
from 8 to 10 weeks. Average ACC work levies will fall to 90 cents from 95 cents. The
HomeStart scheme starts on 1 April, which will enable around 90,000 New Zealanders
to be a ssisted to buy their first homes. New Zealand superannuation will increase by
another 2 percent, meaning that it has increased by 31 percent since April 2008, more
than double the inflation rate.
2788 Oral Questions  1 Apr 2015

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: In light of the primary que stion, when considering how the
performance of the New Zealand economy is translating into benefits for New Zealand
families, has he considered the household labour force survey, which shows growing
unemployment in every region of New Zealand since his Government came to power?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: On “Planet Labour” there was no global financial crisis, but
in New Zealand there was. So, just to remind the member: unemployment went up
pretty sharply in 2008, 2009, and 2010, and it has been dr opping fairly consistently
since. It is still too high, although I might notice that it is significantly lower than
Australia’s, where unemployment is rising, which accounts for the fact that many New
Zealanders are voting with their feet and staying home and coming home because they
have a good prospect of getting a job here.

items.speaker: David Seymour
items.text: How is it that the Government can afford to hand out so much
money and index so many benefits on 1 April, and yet does nothing to index tax
thresholds to inflation for the benefit of the people paying for it all?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: That is a fair question, and, as I think was indicated by my
colleague the Minister for Economic Development last week, that is something that will
be discusse d in the context of future options for moderate tax reductions for New
Zealanders. But I might say that at the moment inflation is around zero and that is
enforcing a discipline on the Government because we are not collecting more tax
because of fiscal dra g, which is a very unusual if not unique set of circumstances. But
this Government is a responsible manager of the Government’s finances, and we will
try to deal with that pressure.

items.speaker: David Seymour
items.text: In light of the Minister’s reference to a u nique set of circumstances
where fiscal drag is low, is this not the perfect time to make the switch and index tax
brackets to inflation?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, it is not the perfect time, but it is the perfect time to start
such a discussion.

items.speaker: Alastair Scott
items.text: How is the Government able to deliver to households the benefits of
sustained growth in the economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: We can deliver some benefits of sustained growth, but I
must say that for most ho useholds it is their workplace that is delivering those benefits,
such as more job security in a growing economy; moderate wage increases year on year,
which over time will lift our average wage by $5,000 to $6,000 over the next 4 years;
and, of course, the general economy, in which interest rates are lower than they might
otherwise have been, and that gives households more opportunity to pay off debt. The
Government can contribute, of course, through its fiscal policy, where we believe that
the measures such as those that are coming in on 1 April are moderate but supportive of
families, and that is some of the benefit that they get from a well-managed economy.

items.speaker: Alastair Scott
items.text: What did the ANZ report say about risks to the economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I think it pointed out some of the risks that have been
discussed in the House before. Part of that is very important, and it is around the
outlook for our trading partners. So with China and Australia, both economies have
some question marks as to their rates of growth. There are also question marks over the
current low commodity prices, particularly in the dairy industry, and the extent to which
they stay low or bounce back to what we would regard as a long -run acceptable and
normal price level. Fortunately, the New Zealand economy is resilient. It has proven it
can deal with headwinds, as it has done over the last 4 or 5 years quite successfully, and
we have every confidence that even if some of these risks eventuate, we will be able to
handle them.
1 Apr 2015 Oral Questions  2789
Accident Compensation Corporation—Levies and Impact on Government
Financial Position
3. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by his statement that “falling off a high horse in Northland can force ACC levies
up”; if so, is that why the Government has set work and earners levies above the levels
recommended by ACC?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I say to the junior leader of the
Opposition—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: —yes and no.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! It is that sort of start to the answer that
does not help the order of this House.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Is his concern about horses in Northland really about high horses, or
well-run thoroughbreds?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: All I know is that in 2014, like in 2011 and 2008, we went off
to the races and we won big time.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Given that ACC itself has recommended against the $350 million
overcharge, why is National forcing Kiwi businesses and workers to pay excess ACC
levies that even ACC says it does not want or need?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I would remind the member, firstly, that the ACC board often
makes a range of recommendations. In 2010- 11 the Government actually increased
ACC levies by $1.137 billion less than what was recommended by ACC. Today,
actually, I read an interesting quote that said the following: “The Employers’ levy
remains the same at an average of 90 cents per $100 of payroll. Although ACC
recommended a reduced levy rate of 85 cents, the government decided there was a need
to give employers more stability in levy rates from year to year, as well as building up
reserves.” That was from Lianne Dalziel, Labour’s ACC Minister in 2002-03.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Moving on 13 years to this year, is it in the public interest,
particularly the interests of levy payers, for ACC to take more in levies than it needs and
more than it wants when its work and earners accounts are already overflowing; if so,
how?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I take it from the member that he is thinking that we should do
as he says, not as Labour has done. That seems to be the subtext of his question. I go
back to the point I made earlier. Over time the ACC board has made a series of
recommendations. The Government adopts what it thinks is right. It is on track to do
that. As you know, from 1 April —today—there have been further cuts. There will be
more on 1 July, I think from memory. It is on track for about $1.5 billion worth of cuts
in the last 12 to 18 months alone.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Given his failure to end his ACC rip- off this year, will he now
commit to cutting next year’s ACC levies by at least $350 million in the coming
Budget; if not, why on earth not?

items.speaker: Rt Ho n JOHN KEY
items.text: What the Government will do is get a further set of
recommendations, as is required by law, from the ACC board and consider those in
context. But I would make a couple of points, and that is that if one looks at ACC and
the factors that drive i ts levy recommendations, one sees that there are a number of
moving factors in there, including the discount rate. So the member just better be a little
bit careful what he wishes for, because the ACC board may well come out with a
recommendation he does not like.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why did he fail to tell New Zealanders that most of his ACC
reductions were just reversing his Government’s earlier levy hikes, put in place because
2790 Oral Questions  1 Apr 2015
of Nick Smith’s creative and fake crisis as the smokescreen for pri vatisation? Why does
he not reverse those? Tell the truth.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It is true that this Government put up ACC levies when we
first came into office. [ Interruption] Interestingly enough, the member says
“unnecessarily”. The recommendation from the board, which, by the way, he wants us
to adopt this year, was to put them up by $1.3 billion, and the reason the board wanted
them to go up by so much was that Labour left ACC unfunded and broke. What a
disgrace from the Labour Opposition. What a disgrace.
Housing Market—Subsidies and Median House Prices
4. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green) to the Minister for Building and

items.speaker: Housing
items.text: Does he agree with the Reserve Bank Governor’s advice in relation to
proposed changes to the Welcome Home Loan Scheme and KiwiSaver Subsidies that
“over the longer term, subsidies have the potential to add to existing house price
pressure in what is a highly overvalued market”; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The member
overlooks two important facts in the advice from the Reser ve Bank Governor. The first
is that it was dated 18 June and was directed at an earlier version of the HomeStart
package in which it was proposed to increase grants for buying existing homes by 50
percent. The final HomeStart package agreed by Cabinet on 1 8 August took this advice
into account and left the grants for existing homes as is. The second fact is that the
member does not include the Reserve Bank Governor’s complete advice, in which he
said: “The targeting of a higher subsidy for new homes would be expected to have a
positive effect on new housing supply.” Consistent with this advice, the final package
doubled only the subsidies for new housing supply.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: With regard to new housing supply, does he agree with the
Reserve Bank Governor that increasing these subsidies will result in “higher margins
for developers and builders”?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Again, the member is being cute with his quotation. He
forgot the word “might” —forgot the word “might”. Actually, it is our view that by
providing a grant to the homeowner, we can have confidence that they will shop around
and get themselves the very best deal. We do not agree with those members’ policy, and
that is that they do not trust homeowners and they  want the State to build the houses
they think homeowners want.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: By how much have median house prices risen in Auckland
since his Government took office?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: There is new data on house prices out today. It shows that
in the course of the 6 years of this Government house prices in Auckland have gone up
by an average of 5 percent per year. It is interesting to compare that with what house
prices went up by on average under the previous Government, where the average was
10 percent per year, or double —that is, house prices were going up an average of
double during the previous Government’s 9 years.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is the Minister aware that the median house price in Auckl and
has gone up under his Government by more than $250,000, and does he think that is
sustainable?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: No, I do not think it is sustainable. That is why this
Government has passed more legislation in respect of housing than any Government in
the last 20 years.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Tinkering and photo ops.
1 Apr 2015 Oral Questions  2791

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The member says that it is tinkering. I would suggest that
the special housing areas legislation —which has opened up land for 34,000 houses;
more land has been opened up in Auckland in the last 12 months than in the last 10
years—is the sort of policy that is required. The biggest cost increase in Auckland has
been in the price of the section, and it is actually the sort of policy that is advocated
around a tight metropolitan urban limit, which the Green Party supported, that is at the
core of Auckland’s house prices.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: In light of the fact that this Government has now been in office
for more than 6 years, what responsibility does he take for the fact that median house
prices in Auckland have increased by more than a quarter of a million dollars, and how
on earth are people supposed to afford those kinds of house price increases?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The first point I would make is that when we came to
Government New Zealand was building 1,000 houses per month. The latest figures,
which came out yesterday, show that we are building 2,000 houses per month, and an
increased supp ly is at the core. I had also missed this: New Zealand is a much more
popular country to live in. We do not have 50,000 people a year leaving to Australia. As
a consequence, there is more demand. We on this side of the House welcome that, but
we also accept the challenge that we have to build a lot more houses, given that we are
now a much more popular country to live in.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he think that giving $10,000 or $20,000 subsidies to a
couple to buy their first home outweighs  the $250,000 increase in the price of housing
in Auckland, and is it not only a drop in the bucket compared with that price increase?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: In 2007 the previous Government introduced the subsidies
for people to buy a house—at that point $10,000. In that year house price increases were
faster than they are now. The Green Party is on record in 2007 saying that grants for
first home owners were a great thing. It seems the consistency of the Green Party is that
when the previous Government provides a grant for first home owners it is a great idea,
but somehow when we do that it is not a good idea. That does not sound very principled
to me.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: In light of the $250,000 increase in the median pric e of houses
in Auckland under this Government, will he reconsider his policies of taking no action
to restrict demand from investment buyers through a capital gains tax or from offshore
demand through non-resident foreign buyers?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The evidence is very clear, particularly in the Productivity
Commission’s comprehensive report, that the biggest contributor to increased house
prices is sections in Auckland. They have gone from $100,000 each in 2000 to
$350,000. The key driver of that has been the metropolitan urban limit. That is why this
Government has made the No. 1 priority breaking that metropolitan urban limit, which
we have done with our special housing areas. I wish the member would simply accept
that link between dumb planning policies and high house prices.
Resource Management Act Reforms—Auckland Housing Market
5. PHIL TWYFORD (Labour —Te Atatū) to the Minister for the Environment :
Is he, like the Prime Min ister, relaxed about the effect of dropping major RMA reforms
on new housing supply, and does he agree with the Prime Minister that there are “mixed
views” about how much his reforms would have addressed Auckland’s housing
shortage?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I have checked, and the
Prime Minister’s comments were specifically in respect of the changes to sections 6 and
7, of which there are mixed vie ws. The Prime Minister equally made the point: “the
procedural changes are very important.” For instance, the Housing Accords and Special
2792 Oral Questions  1 Apr 2015
Housing Areas Act, which bypassed the more clumsy procedural parts of the Resource
Management Act, has freed up land s upply for 43,000 homes in Auckland. This law
expires in September next year, and our Resource Management Act reforms need to
ensure ongoing land supply and residential development.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: When the Prime Minister said yesterday that there are mixed views
about how his Resource Management Act reforms would have addressed the Auckland
housing shortage, was this because Nick Smith says that the Resource Management Act
is to blame for the rising cost of housing and hardly anyone else agrees?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Every member of this House knows that the Resource
Management Act is the primary law that governs the creation of sections. The price of
sections in Auckland has gone from $100,000 in 2000 to an average of $375,000 today.
If we are serious about improving house prices, we have to focus on section prices, and
the Resource Management Act is critical to resolving that issue.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Which quote best describes his Resource Management Act
announcement in January: “An attempt to manipulate public sentiment with
unsubstantiated claims, rhetoric, and at times misleading analysis.”, that was the
Listener; “[jumbled] together anecdote and slogans, common  sense, and windy
abstractions.”, that was the Domin ion Post; or “A blunderbuss attempt to obliterate the
RMA.”, that was Radio New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I could cite hundreds of sources that received this
Government’s Resource Management Act reforms very positively, and I actually  even
note—

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Name one!

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: —oh, name one—that Labour’s environment spokesperson
says that Resource Management Act changes are important. So even Labour accepts
that if we are serious about addressing housing affordability, Resource Management Act
reform is an important part of the package.

items.speaker: Joanne Hayes
items.text: Have any changes been made to the Resource Management Act that
have negatively impacted on land supply and housing affordability in Auckland; if so,
when were those changes made?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: At the heart of the Auckland housing issue is land supply
and the rigid boundary imposed by the former Auckland Regional Council’s
metropolitan urban limit. That has seen s ection prices in Auckland go up by 300
percent. District and city councils had to have regard only for the metropolitan limit
under the original Resource Management Act, but changes made in 2004 meant that
regional councils’ plans trumped local council rul es. This change turned the
metropolitan urban limit into a straitjacket, saw section availability drop dramatically,
and saw undeveloped land prices inside the metropolitan urban limit increase, in some
cases by a hundredfold.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Does he agree with John Armstrong in the New Zealand Herald that
he was using the Resource Management Act as a smokescreen; if so, was he using
housing to disguise his weakening of the Resource Management Act’s environmental
principles or was he using the Resource Management Act to distract from his failure to
fix the housing crisis?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The Productivity Commission produced a comprehensive
report on housing affordability. It said that at the core of what this Parliament mu st
address, if it is serious about making housing more affordable, is those planning rules
within the Resource Management Act. I simply say to the member opposite that

Superannuation—2015 Annual General Adjustment
6. TODD MULLER (National —Bay of Plenty)  to the Minister for Social

items.speaker: Development
items.text: What is the Government doing to support people receiving
superannuation in retirement?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Today superannuation
and veterans pension payments have increased by 2.07 percent as a result of the annual
general adjustment. This increase will see married superannuitants receiving  an extra
$11.68 each week, while those living alone will receive an extra $7.59. This
Government has committed to keeping the married couples superannuation rate to at
least 66 percent of the average wage, and this increase is the result of rising wages i n a
growing economy. Since 2008 superannuation and veterans pension payments have
increased by 31 percent, double the rate of inflation, allowing superannuitants to enjoy a
better standard of living in their retirement.

items.speaker: Todd Muller
items.text: What impa ct does the annual general adjustment have on
beneficiaries?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: In 2011 this Government passed legislation to increase
benefits annually in line with inflation. As a result, benefit payments to around 440,000
New Zealanders will also increase today by 0.51 percent. The thresholds for the
community services card have also increased. This increase benefits thousands of New
Zealanders receiving a range of assistance through Work and Income and StudyLink,
and it ensures that benefits keep pace with increased living costs.
Regional Economies—Northland
7. Dr DAVID CLARK (Labour —Dunedin North) to the Minister for Economic

items.speaker: Northland

every single region of New Zealand is higher than when the Government took office in

Income Gap, Parity with Australia—Minimum Wage
8. DENISE ROCHE (Green)  to the Minister for Workplace Relations and

items.speaker: Safety
items.text: What is the size of the gap between the New Zealand minimum wage hourly
rate and the Australian national minimum wage hourly rate?
Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE (Minister for Workplace Relations and
Safety): I am pleased to advise that today the gap between the two countries has closed,
thanks to the increase in the minimum wage, which will put $1,000 a year in the pockets

Zealand is a little difficult, due to changes in the exchange rate and the fact that
Australia has minimum rates for youth and the disabled. But if we take the adult

Zealanders who realise the grass is actually greener on this side of the Ditch and they

Paid Parental Leave—Increases
9. Dr PARMJEET PARMAR (National)  to the Minister for Workplace

items.speaker: Relations and Safety
items.text: How is the Government helping to support new parents?
Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE (Minister for Workplace Relations and
Safety): As part of Budget 2014’s $500 million investment in the well -being of N ew
Zealand’s children and families, we announced that the Government would improve
paid parental leave to help young families get ahead. This is happening in two steps, and
the first came into effect today, with paid parental leave increasing from 14 to 16 weeks.
From 1 April next year, this will be increased by a further 2 weeks, to a total of 18
weeks’ paid leave. This Government wants to support families in making the choices
that are best for them, so we have increased the parental tax credit, which has  not been
raised since 1999. The tax credit is paid when low and middle -income working families
who are not on a benefit and who do not receive paid parental leave have a new child.
From today that parental tax credit  increases from $150 a week to $220, and the
payment period has been extended from 8 weeks to 10 weeks.

items.speaker: Dr Parmjeet Parmar
items.text: What other changes are in the pipeline with paid parental
leave?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I will be introducing legislation to the House this
year that will extend paid parental leave eligibility to more workers and increase the
flexibility of the scheme. These changes will include extending parental leave payments
to non-standard workers such as casual staff and those who have recently changed jobs;
extending entitlements to primary carers other than biological parents, such as
permanent guardians, Home for Life carers, whāngai, and grandparents; and enabling
employees to take their leave mor e flexibly by mutual agreement with the employer.
Each year more than 26,000 people take paid parental leave. Our changes will make it
easier for thousands of New Zealand parents to take more time off work to spend with
their newborn child if they wish, and will provide extra support for young families at an
important and challenging time.

items.text: Why did National vote against funding 26 weeks’ paid parental leave
for babies born with a disability, those born prematurely, or to the parent s of multiple
births, at a cost of just $6 million, when only 3 weeks later the Government found $70
million to fund the Northland bridges election bribe?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: There is already a great deal of assistance for
parents of multiple -birth children. The Government currently provides payments for
home help to assist with multiple birth s, Working for Families tax credits provide four
types of payments for families with dependent children, and there is a whole range of
extra financial support for families in special circumstances, such as accommodation,
childcare, and other grants. For families wit h a new baby with a disability there is a
child disability allowance to help parents meet the additional costs, and a whole range
of initiatives from disability support services that provide wraparound services for these
families.

10. MAHESH BINDRA (NZ First)  to the Minister of Corrections : Is he satisfied

corrections facilities?

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA

privately run prisons, and given the recent death of a prisoner in custody —with
condolences to the family —what mechanisms are in place in all of New Zealand’s
corrections facilities, both public and privately run, to keep staff and prisoners safe from
prison assaults?

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU -IIGA
items.text: As the member knows, staffing levels for
residential units and operational support functions at each publicly managed prison were
set in 2001. Those ratios looked at the staff -to-prisoner ratios for remand prisons, which
were set at 1:15; for high to medium prisons at 1:15; and as well for youth prisons at

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU -IIGA
items.text: For Serco —I am getting to that, ma’am—it is
based on the output and the outcomes that Serco is able to do. In the last prison
performance table, might I just add, Serco’s Mt Eden Corrections Facility was the most
exceptional prison based on core security, internal procedures, and its rehabilitation
score. So it is clear that despite the fact that we have that private prison, it is one of the
highest-performing prisons in New Zealand.

items.speaker: Kelvin Davis
items.text: So what is being done to reduce the numbers of assaults on both
inmates and staff in correctional facilities?

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU -IIGA
items.text: As that member knows, prisons are extremely

escalation techniques to all front -line officers. We have trialled on -body cameras, and a

response team at Spring Hill prison, which was implemented today.

Tax System—Reforms for Businesses
11. IAN McKELVIE (National—Rangitīkei) to the Minister for Small Business :
How will small and medium businesses benefit from the Government’s proposals to
simplify the tax system?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: Small and medium sized
businesses will benefit from a simpler and modernised tax system. The Government is
considering possible improvements to simplify the tax system for businesses by
streamlining the collection and calculation of PAYE, GST, and related information, by
integrating these obligations into various business processes —things such as leveraging
new technology and simplifying calculation for provisional tax based, perhaps, on real -
time information. I encourage small and medium enterprises to make a submission on
these very good proposals. These initiatives will make for a more modern, efficient, and
flexible tax system, once again demonstrating why this Government is better for
business.

items.speaker: Ian McKelvie
items.text: How are small and medium businesses benefiting from the changes

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: Sma ll and medium businesses, whether in rural areas, in the

Government has made to the tax system, including lower company tax rates, lower
personal income tax rates, and maki ng tax compliance easier for businesses through
initiatives such as myIR online accounts. Small and medium businesses are also
benefiting from other changes by removing unnecessary reporting requirements, cutting
red tape, and improving infrastructure.

items.speaker: Hon MAGGIE BARRY
items.role: Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage
items.text: I move, That
the House take note of miscellaneous business . I intend, in my call today, to reflect on
New Zealand’s WW100 programme. The centenary of the First World War officially
commenced in August last year and is going to be continuing through until 2019. It will
commemorate a range of events that are international and national, and that are also
1 Apr 2015 General Debate 2801
community based. There are some 850 community events that have been organised so
far, and the details are on the website for WW100, which comes out of my ministry.
One hundred years on, the centenary of the First World War is an immensely
significant event. It was really the beginning of the Anzacs —the Australian and New
Zealand Army Corps—and the ties that bind New Zealand and Australia were formed at
that time. It has been said of both countries that our nationhood is built on the war effort
and on the sacrifice of our forebears 100 years ago.
The effect that the First World War had on this country is apparent in very many
ways, from our individual family histories to how we see ourselves as a nation and how
we are seen by others. The so-called Great War is the cornerstone of our friendship with
Australia. Strengthened at Gallipoli, in the Middle East, and on the Western Front, the
Anzac bond is a fundamental part of the identity of both of our nations. In the official
history of Australia in the Great War, the Australian historian Charles Bean wrote of the
diggers—and it equally applies, I feel, to the New Zealand soldiers —that their creed
was the miners’ and the bushmen’s: “Stand by your mate”. Cricket games
notwithstanding, we have done that eve r since. Our partnership, which was forged in
adversity, is as strong as it ever was. A hundred years on, the centenary of the First
World War is an immensely significant event to all of us.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Why are you reading this?

items.speaker: Hon MAGGIE BAR RY
items.text: It is something that we need to take note of, and with
some respect, which is not shown currently by the members opposite. When we reflect
on the legacy of service and sacrifice and on how that war made an impact on the
society we kn ow today, we need to reflect very carefully on the number of New

items.speaker: Zealanders that went across to Europe
items.text: 100,000 New Zealand men went across to
Europe. At the time, that was around 10 percent of our population. We went the farthest
and our casualties were h igh. Our rates were something like 60 percent of those who
went. They were wounded, they were killed, they came back, and some of them died as
a result of their injuries. More than 18,500 men lost their lives. That is a truly chilling
and staggering figure, and I think that as we commemorate the next 4 years, it is a figure
that we need to keep in our minds.
The soldiers, though, who returned from the wars did not necessarily tell their stories
to their families or to the people whom they knew and loved. T hey found their
experiences far too hard to talk about, and for those people —some of them who could
never share their stories —that challenge has been taken up now by some of the
commemorative events that are being featured in New Zealand over the next 4 years.

items.speaker: I give you one example
items.text: Sir Peter Jackson’s The Great War Exhibition , which is
going to be at Wellington’s old Dominion Museum. I have seen a preview of it. It is a
truly sensational exhibition and there is much in that to be proud of. It tells the s tory of
the individual men and women—the men who went away to the war, and the women
who stayed behind and kept the home fires burning. When you look at these unspoken
stories through the theatricality of the Hollywood creative genius of Sir Peter Jackson,
we see, essentially, that our nation reveals itself as the men and women who were the
way we were, and who are the way we have become.
So we look at the Pukeahu National War Memorial Park in Wellington. That is
officially opening on 18 April 2015. I was at the dawn ceremony last week. It is a very
special place, and in it there will be a context of what we call the war memorial gardens.
The Australian one—it is fitting—is the first of those. We will have the Prime Minister
of Australia, along with our Prime Minister, present at the official opening. That will be
followed by gardens and memorial tributes from the United Kingdom, from the United
States, from Canada, from France, and also from other countries that we are in
discussion with. Expect over the ne xt 4 years, and then beyond, that many of the
2802 General Debate 1 Apr 2015
conflicts that our New Zealanders have been involved with over a very long period of
time will be commemorated there.
The ceremonies that will take place on 20 April really set the tone for what will
happen through an action-packed Anzac week, when people will come from all over the
world to stand with us to commemorate our role and our experiences in the war. As the
Minister responsible for the World War I commemorations, I have been deeply
impressed by the work that has been done at Pukeahu. It is our major commitment to the
legacy projects of World War I, but it not our only project. More than $10 million has
been spent on the programme—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: It is a privilege to be back, as
the member of Parliament for Northland. Five weeks ago the PM said that we would not
stand. Then, when we did, he said that we had zero chance of winning. And then some
of my media friends said that it was a joke and a stunt —some have had the good grace,
of course, to recant since then.
So let us start with an olive branch to Mr Key and the Government. If their Resource
Management Act reforms are in the interests of New Zealand’s growth and environment
and the hard -working people who make up our brilliant primary industries and the
forgotten regions, then we in New Zealand First will give them serious consideration.
The problem is that they have never —not once—had the decency to call us, despite
their Michelle Boag’s deplorable attempt on Q+A  to say otherwise. So we warn them
that if thes e reforms stoke the Auckland property bubble that is keeping interest rates
high, and with it the New Zealand dollar —a dollar that is crucifying our productive
sector, being close to parity with the Aussie, at record highs against the euro, at 8- year
highs against the yen, and stuck in the high 70c range against the greenback—then,
Messrs Key, Smith, et al. We will not, and we cannot, help you.
Last Saturday Northlanders went up to this Government’s flagstaff and chopped it
down. In doing so, they sent a m essage on behalf of Southland, the West Coast,
Marlborough, Whanganui, Manawatū, Wairarapa, Hawke’s Bay, Gisborne, the Bay of
Plenty, the Waikato, and elsewhere. That message is this: “It’s the economy, stupid.” It
is not a two-tiered economy. It is not all about Auckland. New Zealand excels when our
regions excel, but if they are treated like second -class citizens despite generating this
country’s wealth, they are going to rebel.
Look at Northland’s neglect: the lowest median income in New Zealand; over 778
one-lane bridges; 1,100 kilometres of unsealed roads in Kaipara, with 70 percent of the
roads in the far north unsealed, and with the people who complain being threatened by
bully-boy National MPs; a rail line that is so bad that it takes almost 5 hours  to shift
goods south to Auckland; and a place where you can forget 4G because a simple
cellphone call is itself a trial.
While billions of dollars are being poured into the commuter rail in Auckland and
Wellington, this Government cannot spare $6 million to fix the Napier to Gisborne line,
or to join the north line with Marsden Point. What that says about the regions in this
Government’s priorities is not lost on them. Although we know about Northland’s
bridges, the West Coast has over 49 of them on State  highways, and, yes, we will ask
the district councils how many are classed as local roads—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Don’t be silly, Winston.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Do not shout here like Maggie Barry did at our
meeting in Dargaville, in the Methodist church. She came up. She was shouting. She
had to be stopped by the chairman and all the crowds. There she was, like all of the
National Party, and I said to her: “Look, Maggie, we can paste you any day in the
House. Don’t  come up here, where we are loved, and expect to be getting a decent
1 Apr 2015 General Debate 2803
audience.” She got told off by everybody, including the chairperson, and she was
driving there in a ministerial car—all a waste of taxpayers’ money.
All these other Ministers and backben chers were making phone calls and putting up
hoardings, and when I saw them putting up hoardings I thought to myself: “You guys
are finished.”—you guys are finished. When I see hard- working men like Alfred Ngaro
and I see Mr Mark Mitchell from next door putting up hoardings, I know that the
National Party has collapsed up north.
Look, we asked the good people there to send a message and, boy, they did. And
now we have got the National Party in so many days —just 4 days —later, it cannot
remember it.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: What’s the message, Clem?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: The message, Gerry, is that it is over time for you.
The message, Mr Brownlee, is that they have had enough of your neglect. They have
had enough of your arrogance. They have had enough of being forgotten. They have had
enough of being marginalised, Cinderella -ised, and forgotten, and those hundreds of
thousands of people who have created our wealth, not just in Northland but around this
country, are goin g to make sure they get a fair go in New Zealand’s political and
economic future. They cannot wait for the next election, and— you know something —
nor can I.
Mr Key was asked all those questions yesterday and today, and it may as well have
been—as they say in the information technology industry—vapourware. Our message to
rural and provincial New Zealand is this: help is on its way. Help is on its way. I know
that the National Party has tens of thousands of members, maybe hundreds of thousands
of members, who are now also very pleased to see that we are back.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I deliberately waited
to raise this point of order so as not to interrupt the member’s speech.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Can I have the point of order?

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: The point of order is —and I am looking to you to protect the House
and the Opposition—that there is a Standing Order that states that members cann ot
move from their own seat to another seat to better interject and break up another
member’s speech. You sat there and you did not deal with Mr Brownlee.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member is right. If a member had moved, I had not notice d it,
so it may have actually been helpful if the member on this occasion had raised the point
of order when it happened. [ Interruption] Order! I am still on my feet. I do not think
that it in any way disrupted the performance by the Rt Hon Winston Peters.  He was
enjoying the interjections as much as most of the rest of the House.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I
just want to apologise to the Rt Hon Winston Peters for interrupting his speech. I was
merely trying to defend myself from the vicious attack I was subjected to!

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: We will now return to the debate.

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Today is a very,
very good day for New Zealand families. There is an increase in the minimum wage, the
sixth in a row under this Government, even in straitene d times, and this now means that
those who are on the minimum wage have $5,700 a year more in their income. Paid
parental leave now goes up, and I will be introducing measures to broaden and deepen
the well of people who will benefit from paid parental lea ve from next year. There have
been increases in superannuation and veterans’ support payments, as announced by the
Minister for Social Development, one of many, many more benefits still to come. The
increase in the payment for GP visits for those under 13 will be coming in this year,
along with free breakfasts in schools, and warmer, drier homes. This Government cares
for New Zealand families.
2804 General Debate 1 Apr 2015
But I want to touch briefly on the crime statistics that came out this morning. For the
fifth year in a row data r eleased today shows that recorded crime has dropped again. If
we had continued on the trajectory we were on in 2009, there would have been 100,000
more crimes. That is a reduction of 100,000 victims and their families compared with
where we were heading. T here has been a 7.8 percent drop in Canterbury and a 9.4
percent drop in Waikato. There are concerning trends around sexual and family violence
and it is very hard to discern between an increase in the incidence of reporting and an
increase in the incidence of crime. And this is a very poignant backdrop to
acknowledging that there are challenges in many ways in respect of that, but I want to
acknowledge the New Zealand Police for further reductions in reported crime.
I want to touch today on the spirit of Anzac. The Cricket World Cup has come and
gone. The din has died down. The Northland by -election is over, and to the victor the
spoils. We are going to go into an adjournment. During that adjournment we are going
to have one of this country’s most poignant  commemorations—the 100th anniversary of
the Gallipoli landings on 25 April 1915. It was my great honour as the then Minister of
Veterans’ Affairs in 2014 to attend the 99 th anniversary of Anzac Day at Gallipoli. It
was a remarkable experience. The Dawn Service, which commenced at around 5 a.m.,
was against the backdrop of what was exactly the weather on that day 99 years earlier. It
was calm. It was sombre. It was completely  incongruous to the sort of mayhem that
must have faced New Zealand and Australian soldiers as they approached what is now
known as Anzac Cove. The incongruous nature is due to the fact that we have been
brought up with an image of Anzac Day and the Gallipoli campaign that is from grainy,
black and white and sepia photographs of a barren land and emaciated and injured and
unwell soldiers dug into the side of mountains. But those who have been to Ҫanakkale
in the Gallipoli Peninsula will know it is a beautif ul place, a peaceful place, a place
where thousands of Australians and New Zealanders lie buried and are looked after and
looked over by the Turks, who are now our friends—once our enemy.
We are going to go into a commemoration that does not glorify war, and indeed we
should not, but it does acknowledge the tremendous sacrifice that thousands of young
men and women, who went and never came home, made for this country. I think we
need to stop and reflect on that, and on the theatres of war that are resplendent around
this Chamber, and just remember the heavy burden that we have to bear when we make
decisions to send our young into harm’s way. Those challenges remain—

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: And sometimes you shouldn’t. Sometimes you should say no.

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WO ODHOUSE
items.text: That is right. Let us just remind ourselves that
the same number of soldiers who will be deployed in Iraq, to support freedom and to
control a heinous threat to New Zealanders here and abroad, died every 3 days on the
Gallipoli Peninsula. I think we need to reflect on that and pay an appropriate tribute. I
really look forward to the centenary commemorations.
Debate interrupted.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt this
debate. Subject to discussions among party whips I seek leave for the House to rise
tomorrow at the conclusion of the remaining stages of the legislation arising from the
Objectionable Publications and Indecency Legislation Bill.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for the House to rise after that particular legislation
nominated by the Minister. Is there any objection? There is no objection.
1 Apr 2015 General Debate 2805
Debate resumed.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: I have to say that what was once
characterised as a dirty, filthy, grubby little Government, engaging in dirty, grubby,
filthy little tactics —as it tried in Northland—what we now have is a sad shadow of its
former self. And the resident Elvis Presley impersonator sits there giggling because he
is about to break out in a rendition of “Suspicious Minds” because that is what is
governing the Cabinet and the National Party caucus now, as the finger of blame rotates
around the caucus room and the National Party wonders who is responsible.
We observe today the stunning achievement of the National Party, which turned what
was a 9,300 majority just 6 months ago int o a 4,000 deficit. That is unheard of in the
history of New Zealand politics —unheard of in the history of New Zealand politics.
The Northland by -election will go down in history as one of the worst defeats of a
political party in this country. The Prime Minister was right to express so many months
ago his concern about the impact on ACC levies of falling off your high horse in
Northland. He might not have thought that it would come, but last week it did. Oh, how
the mighty have fallen—as they say—oh, how the mighty have fallen.
When we cast the finger of blame around let us remember that it was not a single -
handed job; there were many involved. It started with Chris Bishop. Chris Bishop did
not so much fall off his high horse as off his rocking horse. They had a man’s job to do;
they gave it to a boy to do it. So he did not last that long —actually, he stayed up there
for most of the time; we were waiting for him to turn up to Parliament—presumably he
has had his $240 a day deducted from his parliamentary allowance, but we will wait and
see.
Then they put the maestro—the strategic master, Steven Joyce—in charge, and he
knew exactly what to do. This was the man, of course, who gave us great political
achievements such as giving $48 million credit to RadioWorks . Then he was given the
job of fixing Novopay, and 2 years on, how are we doing? We are down to 11,000 faults
each pay period now, but that is better than the 300,000 faults we had 2 years ago. And
then he negotiated the state -of-the-art convention centre —the free convention centre
that was then going to cost us $140 million, and then when the public reacted against
that we now have the less than state -of-the-art convention centre. Who knows what is
going to be put up, but it will be something worthy of the talents of Mr Joyce.
So now we have his big strategy, his big offering: the 10 bridges. You know, I
reckon what happened is that they sat around a campfire in Northland at one of the great
beaches up there, Ninety Mile Beach. They got out the guitars and  started singing the
great cultural classic “Ten Guitars” and that was the inspiration. That was the
inspiration. Ten bridges was going to be the scheme. They thought that having one in
Cabinet was not enough, but having 10 for Northland was going to be the answer. Ten
bridges, and, of course, all it did was serve to remind the Northlanders just how short -
changed they were. That was the great strategic maestro, Steven Joyce— that was his
offering.
Of course, what they reminded the rest of New Zealand of was  just how poorly
served the regions have been under this Government. National still does not get it —it
still does not get it.

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: They get it in New Plymouth. They get it in New Plymouth, Mr
Little.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: When it promised the 10 bridges there was no mention of a
global financial crisis —no mention of a global financial crisis then. But to everything
2806 General Debate 1 Apr 2015
that Labour comes up with, National says: “Oh, it’s the global financial crisis. That
didn’t happen on Planet N ational.” Well, it did happen, and 7 years on regional New
Zealand has nothing to show for 7 years of a National Government—absolutely nothing.
The colleague across the way there reminds me about New Plymouth. Well, he might
want to front up today to the r est home workers at Port View Retirement in New
Plymouth, who have been thrown out of their jobs, and the rest home residents thrown
out of their homes, because the Filipino owners see no future in Taranaki —no future in
Taranaki under this Government. They  have thrown the elderly of Taranaki out on the
streets. They have thrown the good care workers of New Plymouth out on the streets
because they see no future under this Government.
That is what this Government has shown in the regions. Unemployment has ri sen in
every region in this country since this Government took office —every region—because
this Government does not care. When it has the smallest opportunity to do something —
like lower the ACC levies to a realistic level—what does it do? It does not care. It does
not care—that is what characterises this Government. It does not care about the regions.
It has been a wake- up call. National has lost Northland and it will surely lose others as
time goes on.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.role: Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector
items.text: It
gives me great pleasure to rise to my feet after that diatribe to actually point out to the
House that what happened up in Northland at the w eekend was that National got a
message—quite true. National got a message from the people of Northland. It is one
that we are receptive to. It is one that we understand. I might want to also remind the
member Andrew Little, who was previously on his feet, that the people of Northland got
a message from Labour as well. They got the message that Labour does not care enough
to campaign hard for the seat.
Labour had nothing to offer in the way of policies, so much so that it threw Willow -
Jean Prime under the b us. I feel really sorry for that candidate. She worked hard. She
worked hard, but nowhere near as hard as Mark Osborne did, as it turns out. How can
you be completely committed to the task when you are told: “Pull back, pull back.
Don’t say: ‘Vote for me.’  Don’t say: ‘Vote for our policies.’ Say: ‘Vote for the
everlasting promises that come out of New Zealand First.’ ”?

items.speaker: Stuart Smith
items.text: Can they deliver?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: Probably not. The question being put to me is whether New
Zealand First can deliver. Time will tell. Time will tell, but a number of people said to
me: “Look, we might take this opportunity to give a message, but we understand that it
might be a very short-lived message.”
The measures that this Government has taken —and certainly last year’s Budget was
a very strong signal to the families of New Zealand as to how important they are in our
priorities. Our careful economic management during very difficult times has meant,
amongst other things, that we have got 80,000 new jobs on the books. The average
wage grew by 2.5 percent, compared with inflation at 0.8 percent. These are the sorts of
facts you cannot actually argue with, which is why, in fact, the other side of the House
has gone deadly quiet right now. In fac t—[Interruption] Oh look, they are alive —in
fact, they are alive. The average wage is expected to increase by $6,500, to $62,000, by
the second half of 2018.
The circumstances in the by -election gave us a good opportunity to gather our
thoughts around wha t is happening in the regions. Let me tell you that my region, the
Rangitata electorate, certainly understands what low unemployment is. Our biggest
problem is that we do not have enough people to fill the skill gaps. I forgot to say right
at the beginning of my opportunity to speak that the previous member should remember
1 Apr 2015 General Debate 2807
whom to point the finger of blame at when it comes to losses in New Plymouth, given
that member has had plenty of opportunity to experience that.
I do want to comment on the 1 April changes to both benefit and superannuation
payments. There are more than 1 million New Zealanders who are going to feel the
benefit of that. The annual general adjustment is going to see a 0.51 percent increase for
those who require benefits and those who are on student allowances, student loan living
costs, and foster care allowances, and also an increase in the rate of supplementary
assistance. I am sure they will appreciate that, but I am also sure that the work the
Government is doing to free those people f rom reliance on Government assistance is
also being felt throughout New Zealand, and I think that is worthy of mention here.
I also want to comment on the difference that today’s rates will make for
superannuitants and for those on the veterans pension, a s well. It is 2.07 percent. This is
our commitment to maintain the married couple rate at 66 percent of the average wage.
Remember, prior to this Government coming into office, there was no certainty that it
would be at 66 percent. We put that into legisla tion. Before that it hovered. It could be
at 66 percent, but it could go back to 65 percent. We have underlined that in legislation.
We have seen paid parental leave go up on 1 April, from 14 weeks to 16 weeks, but
the note I want to finish on is just the  changes that we are making to the reporting
standards for charities to give New Zealanders trust and confidence in charities, the
27,000 registered charities —$16.8 billion is coming into the total annual income of
those charities. They have tax -free status. They are now reporting on their financials.
There is much more scrutiny on that. They are disclosing more information to the
public, and those changes are coming in as well. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: National did not just lose the Northland
electorate; it was trounced. That was an electorate it had held for 50 years, and it turned
a 9,000 majority into a deficit of 4,000—a turn -round of 13,000 votes. To Jo Goodhew,
if that is her name, who says that that was because of the Labour Party giving it away, I
want to say that Northland was no Epsom. Epsom was a National seat that National
gifted to the ACT Party to keep it alive when it had no support anywhere in the country.
It gifted a National seat. Labour was never going to win Northland, and, certainly, some
Labour voters voted tactically. But a lot of the support that National lost was from
people who had voted National last time and who became disillusioned with a
Government they regarded as tired, arrogant, and ineffectual.
I want to make this point too. This was not, as the National Party would now have us
believe, just a local contest. Northland was covered with electoral hoardings from the
National Party with whose face on them?

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: John Key.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: John Key’s. John Key went up there time and again. The only
time he did not go up there was on election night, when, just as in the case of the Mt
Albert by-election, he left his c andidate floundering and did not stand behind the poor,
unfortunate Mark Osborne, who caught the flack of an electorate that was disillusioned
with National.
Sitting opposite me is Simon “10” Bridges —Simon “10” Bridges —who reflects the
fact that this Gove rnment, in a way I cannot remember in 30 years, went out to pork
barrel Northland to try to buy votes. Ten bridges, $70 million, no cost -benefit analysis,
no prioritisation—an absolute bribe. National thought that the Northland people would
be stupid enough to buy that bribe. Well, Simon “10” Bridges should not have the cheek
to be speaking up and interjecting now. He was part of the failure of this National
Government, as was John Key, and as was the maestro Steven Joyce, who
masterminded National to its worst ever defeat in a by-election. The killer blow was not
delivered by anybody but National members. They shot themselves in the foot. They
2808 General Debate 1 Apr 2015
reminded Northlanders how long they and the other regions had been neglected, and
they thought that Northlanders were stupid enough to fall for the bait.
Well, I say that New Zealanders have had enough of the game -playing, t hey have
had enough of the lack of transparency , t hey have had enough of the sense of
entitlement, and they have certainly had a gutsful of the arrogance. This is the beginning
of the crumbling of the foundations  of this National Government. You can tell by the
agitated state of those backbenchers in the National Party that they know they will not
be here after the next election.
We have seen cyn icism after cynicism. New Zealanders support having a Security
Intelligence Service to deal with terrorism and to deal with economic crime. They do
not support a Prime Minister who rorts the Security Intelligence Servi ce for party
political purposes and who colludes with Cameron Slater . They do not support a party
that lies to the country about what it was  doing. They do not support the Security
Intelligence Service being misused to get a person elected to the World Trade
Organization. The Government is  losing friends all across the world because it was
using the  Security Intelligence Service for the wrong purposes. Finally, they do not
support a National Government that starves the country of money for education, for
health, and for policing—for all of the good things—but that has money to bribe, that
has money to subsidise a casino making a profit, and that has money to splash out on a
local charter school at Whangaruru that is failing, while it is denying kids from
disadvantaged backgrounds the chance to have a full stomach and learn in the classroom
like everybody else.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. I am pleased to stand in this
debate. What a load of rubbish that was from the previous speaker. Let us talk about
bribes, shall we? Let us talk about free student loans, eh? That was one of the biggest
bribes of Labour, was it not? [ Interruption] Oh yeah! Let us talk again about New
Zealand First’s bribes in the Northland by -election. Let us talk about that port. How on
earth is the Rt Hon Winston Peters going to deliver on a port? He is not going to be able
to. Ten bridges—we are going to be able to deliver on 10 bridges. That is what we have
put into our plan, and that is what we are going to do, because we are a Government that
delivers on its promises. We are a Government that when it says it is committed to
doing stuff, it does it. That is what I need to put across.
I have just arrived back from a wonderful conference overseas, in Ethiopia. It was
the Women in Parliaments global summit. I can tell you right now, it opened up my
eyes to many things. I looked around the places that we were fortunate to visit, and one
of the things that I saw was the treatment of old people there. I looked back at New
Zealand, and I thought how lucky we are to have such a great welfare system looking
after our elderly. It has been said many times and it has been heard across the world that
New Zealand, when it comes to its welfare system, has one of the best  in the world,
especially with regard to looking after its elderly. Over 1 million New Zealanders are on
superannuation and will receive an increase in their payments —that is a 2.07 percent
increase in their payments. That is 66 percent of the average wage  for married couples,
as opposed to the average wage.
When I say I was shocked about the elderly, I noticed there were old women in
Ethiopia who were carrying bundles of eucalyptus sticks down the hill. That was what
their job was. When I say I was shocked, I was shocked because once they retired from
that, they retired into town and there was nothing for them —there was absolutely
nothing for them. Every time I looked around the places that I went —I went to some of
the poorer areas in Addis Ababa —I was reminded of that great philosopher Fred Dagg,
who said: “We don’t know how lucky we are.” We do not know how lucky we are.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: He was a great philosopher.
1 Apr 2015 General Debate 2809

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: He was a great philosopher. Then I turn and I look  at something
that is close to my heart, the veterans pension.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: He taught Labour that we can borrow a few million more.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: Ha ha! Then I look to the veterans pension, and I see that it i s a
$60 million package for veterans—to support the new Veterans’ Support Act, which the
Hon Michael Woodhouse is responsible for and which came into force on 7 December
2014. That is great, because I have two grandfathers who fought in the Māori Battalion,
in the pioneer battalion in World War I, and I am sure that as they lay there listening to
their mokopuna standing in this House talking about supporting the veterans package
and all the other things that we do within the veterans sector, they would be very proud
of me as they sit on my shoulders and look across the House.
The Government is also providing $300,000 in grants to the RSA, and all of this has
come through on 1 April. We have also increased the veterans travel mileage rate by 20
percent. That is really important because a lot of veterans like to catch up with each
other and travel from one place to the other —and some of them have long distances to
travel. I am based out of Christchurch East and they have a very strong group,
especially the Māori veterans, which means they do not need to travel that far. But when
I first arrived in Christchurch East there was a tangi on, and the tangi was in the North
Island. So they all gathered together at Ngā Hau e Whā marae and worked out how they
were going to travel north. So this increase in travel payments will help other veterans
throughout New Zealand too, to travel to either tangi or to hui with each other.
From superannuation in the Veterans’ Support Act, I move to employment. With
regard to employment , in terms of the places I went to in Addis Ababa, there were
groups of women who had been funded by their Government to set up their own
businesses within the markets. Those businesses would start on the smell of an oily rag,
and they would grow into big business in Addis Ababa. Some of these were actually
wood-carrying women who carried wood from the top of Mount Entoto all the  way
down into Addis township. That wood was used for housing, it was used for fences, and
it was also used for burning.
One of the things I was also quite amazed at was the innovation in that country. Steel
was at a little bit of a premium for them, especially when it came to building the big
concrete buildings that they are putting together. It is a city that is developing as it go es.
I see the Speaker’s finger circling, but one of the things I just want to say is that I am
really pleased to speak about this. Thank you.

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: I just want to say that today is a clear
indication that the Government has lost its way. It has been so on message the whole
time that it has been in Government, but now Government members are all over the
place. You can see they are in disarray. We can see they are disarray, and they are in
disarray because Northland was the beginning of the end for the National Government.
I want to start by actually congratulating the awesome candidate we had in Northland
and that was Willow -Jean Prime. She did a fabulous job. Des pite whatever that side of
the House might say, we are very proud of our candidate Willow -Jean Prime and we are
looking forward to seeing her in here in 2017. I do not know whether the National
Government can say the same about the candidate that it put up  in Northland. I am not
sure whether National is looking forward to seeing him run again or even being in the
House in 2017, 2020, or any other time moving forward.
Northland was the beginning of the end for the National Government. Northland
showed very clearly that the regions have had enough of being taken advantage of. They
knew when National went in there, promising them 10 bridges and all of these other
things, that actually they had been neglected for a very long time. Here was the pork -
2810 General Debate 1 Apr 2015
barrel politics being rolled out by the National Government. They did not appreciate it,
and National lost because of it.
What we are seeing here today from that side of the House are really the five stages
of grief. Because we like to support our parliamentary colleagues, I thought that in order
to be able to assist with the counselling of that side of the House I would look up the
five stages of grief. What we are seeing is that all of them are at different stages of that
kind of grief model. We have got the first s tage being denial and isolation. And we hear
the denial and isolation—

items.speaker: Hon Nicky Wagner
items.text: Tony Ryall did this speech.

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: —screaming out from Nicky Wagner over there, denying
the fact that National has done anything wrong, denying the fact that the regions have
given up on the National Party. Nicky Wagner is clearly still in the denial phase.
The second phase of the stages  of grief is anger, and we saw that very clearly today
with Simon Bridges screaming at Phil Goff —screaming because he is struggling with
the realisation that he has been tainted by the 10 bridges. He is struggling with the
realisation that he has been made to look like a fool by his leader and his National
Government. So Simon Bridges is clearly going through the stage of anger.
The third stage of grief is the stage of bargaining. I have heard many of the National
Party MPs talking so nicely, off the recor d, about Winston Peters and his win. It is very
interesting. We are starting to wonder whether the bargaining is actually beginning
between National and New Zealand First—well, an attempt at bargaining by National as
it tries to woo Winston Peters and New Zealand First, knowing full well that National
no longer has the numbers to push through things like its Resource Management Act
reforms.
The fourth stage of grief, and we have seen a lot of this today —I think it is really the
stage where a lot of the Nat ional MPs are at—is that stage of depression. We have been
watching from this side of the House as they bow their heads in depression, looking
very sad, sitting there quietly, unsure of what to say, no longer able to even laugh at the
Prime Minister’s failed attempts at jokes. Many on that side of the House are clearly
going through the stage of depression.
The last stage of grief that we hope we can assist the National Government with
getting to is the stage of acceptance—the fifth stage of grief. That si de of the House
needs to accept that Northland was the beginning of the end, that the regions have lost
faith in the National Government, and that in 2017 New Zealand will be voting them
out. Thank you very much.

items.speaker: NUK KORAKO
items.text: Kia ora e te Mana Whakawā. Huri noa i te Whare e
mihi atu ana ki a koutou katoa . I want to bring a bit of decorum back into the House,
particularly because I think we have had enough of Northland. What I would like to do
is just bring it back to two things around Anzac Day and then also the effects of the
announcements made today that National has announced.
So first of all is Anzac Day.  Anzac Day is a day of remembrance, it is a day of
thanksgiving, and also this year it is acknowledgement of the 100 years since the battle
of Gallipoli. I have been over there a number of times. I have been to the Gallipoli
peninsula and to Çanakkale on the Dardanelles, which links the Sea of Marmara with
the Aegean Sea. I have travelled through with many people to Chunuk Bair and to a
number of those battle sites all the way through.
I would like to bring it back now, though, particularly to Rāpaki , the small ancestral
settlement on Lyttelton Harbour. Every year in that ancestral community we celebrate
Anzac Day first with a dawn ceremony, and that has gone on for quite some time. The
reason for that is that when the call -up came for World War I, there we re five who left
from that small village of Rāpaki  and only three came home. So in 1916 the Gallipoli
1 Apr 2015 General Debate 2811
wharf at Rāpaki was constructed as a memorial to those soldiers who never came home
but also to those who did, not just in Rāpaki but right across the spectrum of those tragic
events of World War I.
Every Anzac Day the old, the middle -aged, and the young from Rāpaki  come down
to the Gallipoli wharf and then at dawn we do our memorial celebrations. We go to the
marae for breakfast and then after that we do a hīkoi of 6 kilometres from Rāpaki to
Lyttelton. On the way we pick up a number of people who live in the various towns and
villages en route to Lyttelton. To us that signifies that when our men went overseas
there were no political affiliations; there wa s no race. What they did when they were
there, they did as New Zealanders. That is very significant for us as well, the fact that
