that continues today. We are proud of the fact that in proportion to population there are
more who went away and there are mor e who passed away and were killed over there
compared to almost any other village, town, or city in New Zealand. We are very, very
proud of that. That is the first thing —the acknowledgment. I do acknowledge all of
those on both sides of the House who today  have spoken about the remembrance, the
thanksgiving, and the commemorations that are to come.
The next thing is I want to stay with Rāpaki because Rāpaki to me is a great example
of how the National changes that have taken effect today are helping whānau  and, in
particular, Māori whānau to get ahead. When we look at HomeStart, when we look at
paid parental leave, and when we look at ACC levies, family tax credits, and
superannuation, a cross -section of the people of that small village are affected. That t o
us is actually about having a hand up as opposed to a handout. That was the village of
Ben Couch, and so it is great that National can forge forward and be a party that does
help all New Zealanders, but in particular Māori. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: It is time the Government levelled with the
public on the question of spying. It is time the Government gave an honest account of
how much, in what circumstances, and with what moral and legal justification it
undertakes electronic interception. All the public has been getting lately is a stylistically
shallow assurance from the Prime Minister that he has been advised by the Government
Communications Security Bureau (GCSB) that everything it is doing is within the law.
That is demonstrably lame, to a point of self -contradiction. It is like releasing a murder
suspect on the grounds that he told the police not to worry as he is innocent. On
something as important as the nexus between civil liberties and State power, we deserve
something better than this.
The Green Party recently laid a complaint with the Inspector -General of Intelligence
and Security regarding revelations that the GCSB has been undertaking mass
surveillance through electronic intercepts of people in the Pacific region. There are two
target categories. The first is foreign Governments, and the second is New Zealand
citizens. Spying on Pacific neighbours is offensive. Spying on New Zealanders is,
essentially, illegal. The Prime Minister characteristically parsed the issue,
acknowledging mass collection of data but denying mass surveillance.
Setting aside semantics and confining ourselves to logic, we would not do mass
collection unless there was a contingent intent to do mass surveillance. So the
distinction is meaningless. Certainly, the distinction is lost on the National Security
Agency and also on New Zealanders. It is only the Prime Minister who is impressed by
his own reasoning. Avoiding his resignation required a public soliloquy in the fashion
of Hamlet.
In addition to spying on Pacific friends, the GCSB has extended its services on
behalf of individual Ministers —spying on the Hon Tim Groser’s rivals for the World
Trade Organization job. This included candidates from Sout h Korea, Indonesia, and
Brazil. That too is on the edge of the law or beyond it, as well as being offensive to
2812 General Debate 1 Apr 2015
those Governments. Were they doing the same to New Zealand? In some cases,
perhaps; in others, perhaps not. Either way, it is irrelevant. We are talking about our
own domestic law and political integrity, which has nothing to do with reciprocity. The
Prime Minister has tossed off these actions, in that vapid, blokey way we have come to
know and disown. He beamed, somewhat inaccurately, into the cam eras recently, after
two sessions with the Korean President, claiming the matter had not been raised,
thereby displaying an ignorance of normal diplomatic protocol.

items.speaker: I say to the Prime Minister
items.text: “Are you not concerned by the fact that, despite your
dignified assurance to the world that nations do not give a monkey’s, the Government of
Brazil called in your ambassador for a ‘please explain’ meeting; the Solomon Islands is
undertaking an investigation into who is spying on them; and Tonga has expressed its
disappointment at New Zealand’s actions? You should be.” Moving from the purely
offensive to the potentially illegal, does the Prime Minister stand by his statement
earlier this month that “The law forbids us, other than in very minor circumstances,
from gat hering information on New Zealanders.”? Can he assure the public that the
GCSB is not using a broad definition of the words “private communication” in the Act
to spy on New Zealanders without a warrant?
If the statutory responsibility is on the parties th emselves to display a reasonable
expectation that their communication will not be open to an interception, will it be
sufficient if, in every phone call and email from Kiwi holidaymakers in Rarotonga, they
preface their communication with the words: “I do not expect that our communication is
or should be intercepted.”? Will that be sufficient for the GCSB to click off the
intercept? If 71.6 percent of New Zealanders now believe their private communications
are being intercepted, is that opinion poll in itse lf an instrumental factor in the way the
GCSB would infer what a reasonable expectation must be? Is that not an indictment on
poor legislative drafting?
If I am within the 28.4 percent of Kiwis who like to believe they are not being
intercepted, how do I convey that reasonable expectation to the GCSB? The utterances
by this Prime Minister on the issue are, in truth, not Shakespearean; they are Orwellian.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: Mr Speaker, it is great to be able to
stand up and speak for a few moments. Firstly, as you know, I have been away for a
couple of weeks, up in Northland. It is important to acknowledge our Northland
candidate Mark Osborne. He is a man of tremendous cha racter and integrity. We have
seen an incredible effort from that man to get from 30 percent to 40 percent. Mark, you
are an awesome legend.
I also acknowledge Rose May and Neil Clements, and those local volunteers who
have worked tirelessly for the Natio nal Party. We are a party of volunteers and
supporters, and I want to acknowledge them here today. They did a fantastic job for us.
I want to say to those who voted for us, and to those who did not, that this National
Government will continue to deliver for Northland. We govern for all, regardless of
whether they voted for us or not, and we will continue to deliver. But, ultimately, we
lost, so I do have to acknowledge Winston Peters.
I have known Winston Peters for 26 years. He came to Waikato University when I
was a young fella, to set up the Young Nationals branch. We had 600 people there. I
have to admit that over the years I have admired his charm and his humour, but I have
never admired his vituperative attacks on people as opposed to policy. A great test now
will be whether he has it in him to be collaborative and constructive, or is the
destructive, rock-throwing, negative Opposition MP Winston Peters going to be the man
who represents them for the next 18 months? Well, if it is the latter, it will b e a short 18
months and we will welcome back Mark Osborne in 2017.
1 Apr 2015 General Debate 2813
With regard to messages, I have one for the rabble, the insufferable shriekers on the
other side, who, I have to admit, are currently revelling in our moment of discomfort.
This National Party has the capacity to check and adjust. It has the capacity to listen and
respond. Underestimate our ability to do that at your peril. Provincial New Zealand
needs to see the benefits of our programme in a more tangible way. That was the clear
message that we got.
But I will tell you what is real for New Zealand: paid parental leave increasing from
14 weeks to 16 weeks —that is real; increasing the parental tax credit for lower income
families from $150 a week to $220 a week—that is real; increasing the adult minimum
wage by 50c, to $14.75 —that is real; and reducing ACC levies —that is real. The $218
million HomeStart package; lifting minimum family tax credits, benefit payments, and
superannuation payments—the latter at twice the rate of inflation over the last 6 years—
is real, and we can make that investment because we have a strong economy. We are
focusing on the issues that matter.
What I have noticed over the last 6 months is that with every single thing that this
country has done over the last 6 years, and with single advance we have made, there are
shrieks and sneers from the Opposition. We improve the lives of New Zealanders —we
get a shriek and a sneer. There are 80,000 more jobs —sneer, sneer, sneer. We reduce
unemployment and we get the same thing. We have the greatest result in crime statistics
for basically 10 years —same thing; sneer, sneer, sneer. Well, it is the people of New
Zealand who are creating this momentum, so sneer on if you want to, but on this side of
the House we will succeed on for N ew Zealand. That is happening particularly in
Tauranga. It is an incredible momentum that we have got over there and it is
phenomenal to be able to represent that area along with my colleague the Hon Simon
Bridges.
I just want to give you some examples of what we have achieved collectively —the
people of Tauranga, the Bay of Plenty, and this Government —over the last 6 years.
GDP has lifted 25 percent, and consumer confidence has increased to a 10- year high in
the Bay of Plenty, topping the regional rankings for the first time in 2 years. A lift in
sentiment has propelled household spending up. The number of electronic transactions
is up by 10 percent. The value of building consents issued last year in Tauranga was the
highest for 7 years, and that has driven 200 young people in the Western Bay of Plenty,
in particular, into construction apprenticeships in the Bay of Plenty . Sales volumes are
up 26.7 percent.
The kiwifruit industry —the backbone of the Bay of Plenty —has recovered, and we
are expecting a 70 percent increase in exports, with 4,000 jobs required over the next 6
years. The latest TradeMe statistics show jobs have risen by 26 percent compared with
the previous quarter. The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment has said
that skilled vacancies in the bay grew 20 percent, month on month. These are real
benefits, real outcomes, for the people of the Bay of Plenty , and it is an absolute
privilege to be representing them and to be part of this Government. Thank you very
much.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: I would like to start my
contribution today by congratulating the workers at the Cotton On distribution centre
who today concluded bargaining with their employer, the Australian retail giant Cotton
On, which tried to take away their tea breaks. What those workers did was stand up
against it. The public stood up against it and said: “No way —we don’t like the idea that
those workers should lose their tea breaks.” So not only were the rest and meal breaks
reinstated in the collective agreement but they also got a significant pay rise, and they
got a redundancy clause included in their collective agreement.
2814 General Debate 1 Apr 2015
This tells us a few things. First, it is good to be a member of a union. It is good to
join a union, because joining a union makes sure you get far better terms and conditions
in your collective agreement than the Government would wish you to have. Second, in
the age of social media, I say to employers  who actually want to make use of the
changes to the employment laws that this Government brought in: be very careful,
because the people do not like them. The people of New Zealand do not like the laws
that were brought in; they do not like the idea of workers having their rights taken away
from them. If you are an employer whose business is vulnerable to public opinion, then
you will very quickly feel the wrath of the people of New Zealand. Third, it is important
to know that union membership makes a big difference in public opinion. The
Government was completely out of touch with the people of New Zealand when it took
away their right in legislation to a tea break.
We know that this Government is completely out of touch, because of the by-election
result up in Northland. It went from a 9,000 -vote majority to a 4,000- vote loss in the
space of 6 months. It is the most phenomenal turn- round. And it is because that
Government over there does not pay enough attention to the regions. If you look around
the count ry, regions like Gisborne and Hawke’s Bay, and, sadly enough, Manawatū-
Wanganui, Wellington, Tasman, Nelson, Marlborough, and West Coast all have fewer
jobs today than when this Government came into office. Today, after 7 years of
National Government, ther e are fewer jobs in my region, and in regions like it around
the country, than when National came into office. My region—Manawatū -Wanganui—
and also Taranaki, Wellington, Tasman, Nelson, Marlborough, West Coast, and Otago
all have over 50 percent more peopl e unemployed than when this Government came to
office 7 years ago. Those regions, including, sadly, my own, have unemployment rates
of over 6 percent after 7 years of this National Government. Today regions like mine,
the Chatham Islands, Gisborne, Taranaki, and the West Coast are all receiving less
Government funding for roading than when this National Government first took office 7
years ago.
This Government takes the regions for granted. It expects regional New Zealand to
vote for it but it does not actually do anything to improve the economies in those
regions. The sad thing is that there is massive potential and there is massive opportunity
in every single one of those regions. I appreciate that this Government has embarked on
a project to identify what  those opportunities are —although if it just came and asked,
we would be able to tell it—but what is it actually doing to help us harness those
opportunities, to make the most of them, to get people working, to get people off the
benefit, and to make our r egions productive again? Nothing. The most useful thing that
the National MPs in my part of the country —Ian McKelvie and Nathan Guy—could do
would be to resign. Resign today and let us have a by-election.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: You’ll lose those ones, too.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES -GALLOWAY
items.text: I will tell you what: Simon Bridges would find the
money for the Capital Connection in a heartbeat—in a heartbeat.

items.speaker: Jono Naylor
items.text: It would be better to find some passengers for it.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: Jono Naylor would have somewhere to stand. Jono
Naylor could go and stand in the Rangitīkei. He might have a chance in the Rangitīkei,
and the Government might just fund the Capital Connection if it had a by-election in the
Rangitīkei or in Ōtaki. That is how we could get the National Government to pay
attention to our region and to regions like ours, because it is a sad story of under -
investment and missed opportunities by this Government, which knows that there is
potential in the regions. But it takes the regions for granted, and hopefully the message
that it takes from Northland is that the two -speed economy has got to come to an end.
Pay attention to the regions, National.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
1 Apr 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 2815

sections.heading: Arts Centre Of Christchurch Trust Bill

items.text: Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I move, That the Arts
Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill be now read a second time . As the member in c harge
of the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill, I welcome its second reading. The Arts
Centre holds a really special place in the lives of Christchurch people. Everyone has a
memory of spending time there, whether it was long ago when they were a student,
whether it was more recently at the Court Theatre or the Southern Ballet Theatre, or
whether they have been a residential or a commercial tenant, or perhaps a regular
shopper, a cafe consumer, a movie-goer, or a bar-hopper.
Pre-earthquake, the Arts C entre of Christchurch was vibrant and welcoming. It was
the place to meet, the place to work, and the place to play. It was the creative and
cultural heartbeat of our city. The Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill is an important
element in the ongoing p rotection and preservation of the Arts Centre for the future. Its
purpose is to modernise the governance arrangements of the trust and to set out the
charitable objects of the trust in legislation. It will provide greater certainty around the
original inte ntion of the trust deed and formally recognise the heritage and cultural
significance of the Arts Centre.
The Arts Centre is a magnificent complex. It consists of 24 heritage buildings. The
first date back to 1876 and go right through to 1923. During the earthquakes all but one
of them were very badly damaged. That has resulted in a fantastic but huge restoration
project, which will probably take about 7 years and cost near on $300 million. It is a
programme that has been recognised as the biggest and the most high- tech in the world.
It is going really well. I would like to pay tribute to Andr é Lovatt, the chief executive
officer of the Arts Centre, and everyone who is working on the site for the fact that they
are hoping to be able to deliver it on budget and years earlier.
It was really good that the Local Government and Environment Committee could
visit the site and see the work so that it could understand the importance of this bill. But
the bill is only part of the change that is happening at the Arts Centre. At the same time,
significant planning is under way to let the Arts Centre achieve a vision for the future of
the whole complex. That vision, of course, is informed by the objects of the trust and
recognises the need for the Arts Centre to be financially sustainable in the future.
The new governance structure proposed by the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust
Board follows a comprehensive review and consultation process. Before it drafted the
bill, it carried on conversations with local stakeholders and it also worked with Crown
Law and the Ministry for Culture and Heritage  over a few years. The modernisation of
the governance arrangements will bring the trust in line with currently accepted best
practice. It is vitally important that the trust board has the skills and maintains a strong
set of skills during the restoration phase over the next few years, and also tha t an
enduring governance structure is in place for the repopulation phase and in the future.
Some helpful amendments were recommended by the select committee to improve
the workability of the provisions. It recommended removing the Minister for Arts,
Culture and Heritage from the list of parties to be notified in the event of a vacancy on
the trust board, in order to eliminate any feeling of misperception of the Minister’s
influence on the trust board’s governance. The trust board also considered it import ant
to give certainty to the community that the objects of the trust would no longer be
subject to ad hoc amendments, and that is recognised in the bill.
The reference to stone buildings is entirely appropriate, as it reflects the wording of
the original trust deed and respects the intentions of the original trust. It was noted by
2816 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 1 Apr 2015
the select committee, by majority, that it supports the view of the trust board and does
not recommend deleting the reference to stone in the preamble to the bill or in the body
of the bill. An amendment to the definition of “The Arts Centre” is instead proposed to
clarify the meaning of that term.
The select committee also proposed an amendment to require the trust board to make
the conservation plan of the Arts Centre available  at annual meetings. This is absolutely
supported by the trust board and is consistent with its intended future strategic direction
of open and transparent governance of the Arts Centre. I am advised that the existing
site conservation plan was produced back in 1992, so it has been around for a while and
it is due for updating. The trust has committed to updating that plan for the site
following the completion of the restoration project.
The bill as originally proposed provided for the site to be vested in  the Crown on an
interim basis should the trust ever be wound up. But it is recommended that this be
amended for consistency with other charitable trusts, so now the provisions of the
Charitable Trusts Act 1957 will apply. This is an improvement, I think, to the current
trust deed arrangements and is fully supported by the trust board.
The bill will enable the trust board to continue to be able to recover from the impact
of the earthquakes. It is an appropriate governance structure for the future. It will lay the
foundations for an inspiring public place for the people of Christchurch, for Canterbury,
and for visitors to our city now and for future generations. From the damaged buildings
and the rubble there is a unique opportunity to create a new exciting and vibrant centre
that will be a source of great pride for Christchurch and, I think, for New Zealand as a
whole. In the past, the Arts Centre was one of the city’s most enjoyed tourist attractions.
It was the place that all of us took our visiting friends and relatives to, and I look
forward to being able to do that again very soon.
I would like to thank the Local Government and Environment Committee for its
careful scrutiny of this bill. It is a better piece of legislation because of its work. I would
also like to thank the House for its unanimous, cross -party support. I am extremely
pleased that this bill is back in the House, and I look forward to it being enacted by the
end of the year.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: It is my pleasure to rise to give a
speech on this piece of legislation. It is important legislation, and Labour is happy to
support this bill. I would like to acknowledge the work of the member who has just
taken her seat, the Hon Nicky Wagner, in sponsoring this bill as a local bill. I would
also like to acknowledge the work of the chair of the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust
Board, the Hon Margaret Austin, and the work she has done to save this set of
buildings.
I think that for most Cantabrians, after both the September and the February quakes,
and after questioning whether their family and their friends were safe, their thoughts
turned to what had happened to the Arts Centre buildings and whether or not they were
a set  of buildings that had survived the quakes. For Cantabrians and Christchurch
people, as the previous speaker has just said, there is a deeply personal connection to
this site. This was a site that was gifted to the city in 1973. The announcement was
made in 1973—the year I was born.
I feel a personal connection with this site. Growing up in Christchurch in the 1980s,
everything happened on this site. It was the place of the Dux de Lux, the place where
everyone gathered to have a drink; it was the place whe re there was a market at  the
weekend, when there were no other markets in Christchurch; it was the place where  as a
young teenager in Christchurch , I received my first pamphlet about New Zealand
becoming nuclear-free; it was the place of the Court Theatre;  it was the place of the
Southern Ballet  Theatre; and it was the place of Le Café. This was a place where
1 Apr 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 2817
memories were made in Christchurch . It means so much to the people of Christchurch
that we can save it and that we can have this legislation that enters on to the statute book
the original trust deed, which will ensure that this set of buildings does endure.
The Arts Centre buildings and the trust deed being entered into legislation has
personal significance for me. It was one of the predecessors in my  seat—a predecessor I
share with the Hon Ruth Dyson—the Rt Hon Norman Kirk, who announced the
decision that the university centennial convocation was going to gift, it is said, the
buildings on t he Arts Centre site to the city of Christchurch to be used as  a cultural
centre. But according to Kirk family folklore —I spoke to members of the Kirk family
today—actually, it was a deal done for a dollar  because the university could not simply
gift that land to the city; it needed to be sold to the city. I am infor med by the son of the
Rt Hon Norman Kirk —Bob Kirk, who went on to become a deputy vice -chancellor of
the University of Canterbury —that the university administration, when talk of the
university moving back into the city was raised, would often talk about j ust collecting
the interest on that payment as payment for moving back on to the site.
For Norm Kirk there was a huge significance in this set of buildings being gifted to
the city of Christchurch and becoming a cultural and educational centre for the cit y.
When he announced it, he said that it was a great gift to the city, the province, and the
nation. He expressed his hope that the bodies would use the buildings to draw the
threads of all the cultures of New Zealand and attempt to produce something uniquely
New Zealand in character. I would like to acknowledge the former member for
Sydenham and the work he did in making sure that we have this unique set of buildings
standing in the centre of our city, a set of buildings we can rebuild our city around.
Norman Kirk saw culture as vitally important to New Zealanders and the world in
which they were living. Defending the appropriateness of a politician addressing a
cultural conference in that same year —1973—Norman Kirk said: “Politics is the
conscious projecti on of a country’s identity. The culture is that identity and not
something removed or remote from everyday life.”  I would like us to reflect on those
words, which are as true today, in 2015, as they were when Norman Kirk said them in
1973. He said he saw t he arts as having a very important part to play in our desire to
foster regional cooperation. Again, I would like to endorse those words and say they
have as much to offer us today as they did when Norman Kirk said them.
At the centennial convocation wher e Norman Kirk made the announcement that t he
Arts Centre was being gifted to the city of Christchurch , the gifting was the brainchild
of Professor Neville Phillips from the University of Canterbury. As a PhD graduate
from the history department at the U niversity of Canterbury, I would like to
acknowledge one of the greatest professors of history from that department , the
contribution he and the others have made to the cultural life of Christchurch, and the
foresight that people like Neville Phillips and Norman Kirk had about the value of these
buildings to the city of Christchurch. Neville Phillips certainly saw that.
The gifting of a set of buildings this unique and this special spawned the need for
special rules to be made. Those interested in issues of planning and zoning, and perhaps
even resource management in today’s context, might like to reflect that the first cultural
zone that New Zealand had was this set of buildings . A special part of town planning
was needed to ensure that the heritage fabric of these buildings stayed intact and did not
come under any threat. We in Labour hope that by enshrining the trust de ed in
legislation, as we are with this local bill, we are protecting the heritage value and the
very rich heritage, both social and physical, that these buildings offer to the city of
Christchurch. We want to be sure that these buildings stay.
The Minister in her speech addressed whether or not stone buildings would cover the
whole site. Well, I think I speak for generations of not just Christchurch people but
2818 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 1 Apr 2015
people around the country who have fond memories of times at the Dux de Lux or the
student union, if they were student s at the university when it was on the town site, and
who would like to think that this building will survive the wrecking ball of
Christchurch’s rebuild as well. This is a special building reflecting our character , and is
something that needs to be preserved.
The departmental report that the Local Government and Environment Commit tee
brought back made it clear that the purpose of the legislation was to enshrine the
original purposes of the trust deed, which refer red only to stone buildings. But I would
like to place on the record, and I would like to implore everybody involved in t hat
decision, that it needs to be more than that because the precinct of t he Arts Centre
encompasses more than that to us as Christchurch people. We are told that it would
need special consent as a group 3 building in the Christchurch district plan to be
demolished. But Christchurch people and Cantabrians are only too aware of s ection 38
of the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery A ct, which bypasses many of the protections
we have had for our heritage buildings. We have had 1,240 demolitions within the four
avenues in Christchurch, an area that falls under central government control. Compare
that with the 292 rebuild consents that have been granted in the same space. Of those
1,240 demolitions, 20 percent of those buildings were heritage buildings.
On this side of the House we would like to make it strongly known that we have a
desire to see the heritage fabric of our city retained because our rebuilt and recovered
city needs to value its past. It needs to value the words that Norman Kirk spoke in 1973
when he talked about drawing the threads of all the cultures of our city together to show
something truly unique about our city and our nation. I would like to honour the  people
who have fought for the retention of this site in the past and to thank those of today who
have ensured it will last for many more years to come.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: It is a delight to stand in support of
the second reading of this Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill. As chairman of the
Local Government and Environment Committee, which considered the bill, I got a
sense, as listeners and people observing in the gallery will have had from the two
previous Christchurch-based members who have spoken on the bil l, about the sense of
passion, the sense of commitment, the sense of history, and the sense of ownership of
these buildings that make up this remarkable Christchurch Arts Centre.
I am not a Cantabrian, I am not a person who has spent an awful lot of time in my
life in Christchurch, but every time I visited Christchurch I have been much aware of
the Arts Centre being there. In fact, I can remember 20 or more years ago visiting the
Arts Centre for the first time and being completely overwhelmed by the design , the
history, and the sense of presence of the buildings. So when the devastating earthquakes
of 2010 and 2011 hit the Canterbury region in such a devastating way, it was a shock to
all New Zealanders that the site of the Arts Centre should be so badly da maged in the
way that it was. I think Megan Woods mentioned that there are 24 individual buildings
that make up the Christchurch Arts Centre and that 23 of those 24 buildings were
significantly and seriously damaged.
In the course of the select committee’ s work on this bill the committee was
privileged to actually visit Christchurch and to hear the four submitters in Christchurch
who wanted to have their views made known to the committee. As a result of that, once
we had finished hearing from submitters we  took an opportunity to conduct a site visit.
The site visit was extremely useful and worthwhile. I think members would be truly
impressed if they have the opportunity to go and visit what is regarded as the largest
heritage restoration project in the world currently under way, taking place in
Christchurch right now. It is a 7- year project. It is well under way. There are craftsmen
and stonemasons from around the world using traditional stonemasonry methods for the
1 Apr 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 2819
repair and rejuvenation and rebuild of those heritage buildings, using techniques that
have probably not been used in New Zealand for maybe 40, 50, or 60 years, or even
longer than that. These are truly unique buildings.
I was delighted to hear Megan Woods give the very full history of the site. I was
interested also to note that not one of the submitters mentioned Norman Kirk once.
However, it is clear from her recitation that he was the primary driver in the creation of
the Arts Centre —not wanting to take anything away from other members of the
Canterbury community who over the years have contributed to its success and its
ongoing, enduring place in the hearts of all Canterbury people, and, indeed, probably all
New Zealanders who have had an association with it. It is no doubt that the buildings
hold a very special place in the hearts of Cantabrians, Christchurch people, and, indeed,
many New Zealanders.
So it is important—as the trust chair, Jen Crawford, and the chief executive, André
Lovatt, made clear when they made their submission to the co mmittee—that the
governance for the Arts Centre structure going forward should be a governance
structure that reflects adequately the circumstances that the trust finds itself in today, 40
or more years after the trust was first constituted, and 40 or more  years since the
University of Canterbury exited the site. Now the trust finds itself with a massive
restoration project under way —a project that is going to take a number of years to
complete—and it needs an appropriate, modern, up- to-date, and relevant s kills-based
governance structure in order to see that project through to fruition and to completion.
Secondly, once that project is complete in about another 6 years’ time, the trust is going
to need a governance structure that will ensure the ongoing cons ervation and usefulness
of the site for Cantabrians and for other visitors. To do that, the governance structure
that was set in place originally needed modernising and that is really the purpose of this
legislation.
This is a bill that has been sponsored by my colleague the Hon Nicky Wagner as the
member of Parliament for Christchurch Central, but it is being promoted by the Arts
Centre of Christchurch Trust Board itself. For the trust to actually have the foresight and
wisdom and confidence to bring, promote, and encourage a bill like this gives the House
an indication of the calibre of the current trustees and their recognition that they do have
to be forward-looking and that they do have to look to the future and not just to the past,
because, as with any heritage site, it is the future that is just as relevant as the past in
terms of its care and preservation.
I am delighted that one of the recommendations that the select committee made was
that conservation plans should become part of the annual meetin g structure and agenda.
Each year members of the trust and other associated people who have an interest in the
Arts Centre will be able to get a sense of what the trust is doing in terms of preservation
and conservation, and they will be able to have —as they should do as stakeholders of
that city and that site —an opportunity to participate and be very much part of that. I
want to just quote, if I may, from the submission from the Arts Centre itself, because I
think it neatly sums up the objectives of this bill. The objectives of the trust had
previously been separated from the powers of the trust, and so this bill changes that. It
makes it such that the provisions will truly reflect the trust’s charitable intent, and in a
way that was not previously the case. So those two provisions—which are actually quite
technical and, on the face of them, quite minor —have a fundamental impact on the
ongoing governance, management, and benefit of the whole Arts Centre complex.
There were a number of other changes that the select committee made, and I think it
is worth noting that the select committee process for this bill was a classic example of a
select committee working collaboratively, collegially, and in a cross -partisan way to
ensure that the legislation that was pre sented to us at the first reading actually came out
2820 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 1 Apr 2015
through the select committee process as a better piece of legislation. I am very pleased
to acknowledge that the Hon Nicky Wagner has identified that, and I think all members
of the committee would agree that the process was very good, the intentions were well -
meaning and well -made, and the submitters —all four of them —were generally in
support of the proposed legislative changes. We have made a number of changes. I am
not going to go through them all, but they will, essentially, mean that the Arts Centre is
able to be far more modern in its outlook than it has been in the past. The legal
foundations of the new governance structure will provide a platform and stability for
future trust members and governance  officers of the trust to ensure that the very
significant parts of the history of this site are maintained and protected.
The centre is one of the largest clusters of heritage buildings in the country. We are a
young nation, with not much in the way of longstanding historic buildings. The nature
of our architecture is largely wooden and timber -based, and so a lot of that stone -based
work that was so prevalent and common in the English tradition was not seen in New
Zealand. The Arts Centre in Christchurch actually provides a classic and wonderful
example of what at the time was considered to be a mock little Britain and provide s a
university environment similar to that experienced at Cambridge and Oxford. Members
who take the time to travel to the Arts Centre and have a look at it would immediately
see that the areas where Lord Ernest Rutherford did his significant work were
instrumental in the creation of the site. One of the interesting things that we discovered
in our visit was that a whole lot of history had been uncovered as a result of the
restoration work, and so I was delighted to see some of that.
This is a bill that is  a good bill; it is a bill that the House will, hopefully, endorse
unanimously across the Chamber. It is deserving of that kind of support because it is a
significant piece of governance structure that will mean the Arts Centre will be able to
be governed in a way that is meaningful, proper, and solid going forward. I commend
the bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: It is a real pleasure for me to join the
debate on the se cond reading of the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill. I want to
begin by acknowledging the Hon Nicky Wagner, in whose name this bill is. It is a
private bill, and I know that the Hon Nicky Wagner, who is MP for Christchurch
Central, has had a lot of involvement with the Arts Centre and with the Arts Centre of
Christchurch Trust Board, and she has done a good job of shepherding this bill through
the House. I hope it gets unanimous support from Parliament. That would be a really
nice message to send to Canterbury.
I want to acknowledge Scott Simpson, who I am pretty sure replaced the Hon Nicky
Wagner as chair of the Local Government and Environment Committee. I think there
was somebody in between the two—that is right, there was. I remember now. The Hon
Nicky Wagner used to chair the committee and now Scott Simpson does, and he does a
very good job. I have sat on that committee a number of times. He chairs it with
common sense and rational behaviour, and with a great deal of respect, which I think is
acknowledged by all members of the House. He gets a better outcome, actually, as a
result of doing that. That is not why he does it; he does it because it is his personality,
but it is a good attribute for a chair of a committee to have.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: What a lot of brown nosing.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: I am going to say some nice things about the Assistant
Speaker any minute now. That will really bring the house down. Mr Assistant Speaker
Mallard, I want to commend you on the extraordinarily c ompetent way you chair the
House. I also want to acknowledge Jen Crawford and André Lovatt —Jen is chair of the
trust board—and the other members of the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Board,
1 Apr 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 2821
including a former colleague of ours, the Hon Margaret Austin, who has indeed put a lot
of effort into this bill, as well.
She actually made an early arrangement to invite members of the select committee
that I sit on—the Government Administration Committee—to have an early briefing on
the bill. At that stage she had been told that the bill was going to be referred by
Parliament to the Government Administration Committee. So we all took up the offer.
We got an early briefing, we felt very confident in our preparation to receive the bill at
our committee, and then when it came to the House it was referred to the Local
Government and Environment Committee. We felt cheated, actually. We would have
really enjoyed the opportunity to have had that bill, and I think the members of the trust
board were a bit disappointed that they had to give a briefing to another committee.
More of us knew about the background of the bill. Members have spoken about that
as well as about the history of the Arts Centre. It is quite an interesting position to have
the administration of a centre su ch as the Arts Centre, and, indeed, the governance
structures, determined by an act of Parliament. It is not all that common, and thank
goodness it is not, because we would spend a lot of our time debating those issues, I am
sure. But in this case I do believe that it is warranted. I do believe that the structures that
we have put in place mean that we can have confidence in the governance arrangements
and, indeed, in the future of the Arts Centre. It is one of the most valuable assets that we
have ever had in our city, actually, but particularly now that we have lost so much.
Dr Megan Woods acknowledged her participation as a university student and the
involvement of the Rt Hon Norman Kirk—as MP for Lyttelton, then Sydenham, and
indeed as Prime Minister—in the transfer arrangement from the university to the city of
Christchurch. Indeed, that was a pretty extraordinary gift and transfer. We also have Sir
Ernest Rutherford, a former student on that very site —a great name for all of us to be
proud of. I also want to acknowledge the early student engagement of the Rt Hon Sir Dr
Michael Cullen—I am never quite sure in what order to put all those titles. Michael, a
former colleague of ours in the House, was also a student when the Arts Centre of
Christchurch was indeed the university.
Members have mentioned that there were only four submissions on this bill, and
nobody in the House should imagine that that is because of lack of interest. It is actually
because by the time the bill got here, there had been widespread discussion amongst all
of the relevant parties, and people were confident in the content of the bill.
I do want to make mention of a concern that was raised, because the House needs to
ensure that it is very clear about the response to the submission t hat the select
committee gave —particularly as we go into the next stage, the Committee stage,
because there may well be some calls from Canterbury for us to make sure that the
legislation leaves no doubt of this one point of concern that was raised. That c oncern is
that throughout the bill there are references to historic stone buildings. Of course, that is
blindingly obvious to anyone who has been to the Arts Centre because that is what the
overwhelming majority of the Arts Centre is. It is historic stone buildings, but it is not
all historic stone buildings. There are some buildings that are brick and wood. I just
want to put on record that we want those buildings saved, restored, repaired, and used
for our city’s benefit in the future, as well. The legisl ation, although it refers in that way
to historic stone buildings, does not exclude —as is the desire indicated to us from the
trust board—the other buildings. Of course, that includes the former student union
building as well, which many people will have very fond recollections of.
As I mentioned earlier, one of the reasons why we are very keen to ensure that the
Arts Centre is part of our life in the future is that we have lost so much. Some people,
particularly people from outside our city, say: “Well, of course you have lost so much.
You had huge earthquakes and seismic events.”, and that is undoubtedly the case. We
2822 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 1 Apr 2015
lost a lot as a result of the quakes, but, actually, in Christchurch we have lost a lot
because of section 38 of the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Act. You might think that
this is a bit of an anomaly —how could a part of the legislation designed to support
recovery of a city post -  a traumatic event be part of the destruction of it —but that is
exactly what has happened.
We have had perfectly  good buildings—you know, damaged but perfectly good and
reparable buildings —destroyed by bulldozers and wrecking balls at the whim of the
Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery, the Hon Gerry Brownlee. In one
instance, a magnificent theatre, the Majestic Theatre, which was loved by Cantabrians
as much as the Arts Centre—and I know that the local MP, the Hon Nicky Wagner,
would agree that the Majestic Theatre was an extraordinary and beautiful building—was
bowled over, put in the back of a truck, and dumped. The reason for that was that the
Minister has decided as part of his blueprint for the future that the street that it was on
would be wider. So we lost this magnificent heritage building in order to make the street
wider. I think that is just tragic , I think it is a shame, and I think it was the wrong
decision. So that reinforces our desire to make sure, as far as we can, that similar things
do not happen to as many of our buildings. We have lost too much. We do not need to
lose anything else.
I jus t want to conclude by saying that I also want to acknowledge and thank the
members of the Local Government and Environment Committee. Not only did they hear
the small but important number of submissions with a great deal of interest—in fact,
Scott Simpson, we could have you as a Cantabrian; you sounded really passionate about
the Arts Centre —but they did take the time and trouble. They did not just fly into the
city, have a meeting, and then leave. They took the time and trouble to go to the Arts
Centre and  to become part of the atmosphere, which you cannot help but feel. Mr
Simpson, I am sure you went to the cheesemongers on the way out and got some of
their magnificent cheese. I want to acknowledge all the members who made the effort to
actually go through the Arts Centre and learn a little bit more about the history, about
the damage that was incurred, and then, of course, about the amazing restoration work
that is going on. The use of crafts that are not really part of our everyday life now —and
this was acknowledged by Scott Simpson—is extraordinary. The work that those people
are doing is truly wonderful. I would invite any member of this House to go to see it. It
is absolutely inspirational.
I hope that through the next couple of stages of this bill —the Committee stage and
the third reading —we can give a lot of confidence to the current trust board, the
management, and, indeed, the people of Canterbury that this Parliament understands not
only the importance of the history but also the importance of the f uture of the Arts
Centre. This legislation will give us all the confidence that the Arts Centre has the
backing of Parliament and that its future will be strong. Thank you.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: It is with great pleasure that I stand
and speak this afternoon on the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill. Can I perhaps
start where the honourable member Ruth Dyson also began, by acknowledging you, Mr
Assistant Speaker Mallard, and your guidance of this House. You might not recall it, but
I have followed your political career with interest and, indeed, was involved in one of
your earlier political meetings in Hamilton, when I was a student.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Primary school student?

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: No, not a primary school student.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: You don’t look old enough.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: Exactly. It was at Waikato University. We went to a march
against your then Government, and turned our backs whilst you were talking and
chanted rude things. If I ever knew that one day you would be the Assistant Speaker and
1 Apr 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 2823
I would have to defer to your  judgment, I am sure I would have possibly yelled louder.
It was very good to—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: There are many of us still coming to grips with that idea.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: I am sure.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: It’s a difficult journey.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: It is a difficult journey.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: And I think the member will
now get on with his speech, rather than bring me into the debate.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: I take your guidance, Mr Assistant Speaker. I do want to
acknowledge the Hon Nicky Wagner. I think she clearly articulated her own passion for
this project very well when she spoke earlier and, as people have said and as members
have said, she has guided this through the process to date.
I also do want to add my voice to the chorus of approval that we have heard from the
other side for the chair of the Local Government and Environment Committee, Mr Scott
Simpson. I can only echo that. He is a  tremendous chair and a tremendous local MP,
but, in particular, he has shown real flair and élan in respect of the way he is
approaching his chairmanship of this committee. It allowed us, of course, to spend a
good time as a select committee reflecting on  the issues that were in front of us in
respect of the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill.
There has already been some commentary in respect of the extraordinary day we had
in Christchurch a couple of months ago. The select committee obviously went down to
hear the various submitters give their perspectives on this bill and, as has been noted,
we then spent some time actually going and having a look at the Arts Centre precinct
itself. I was hugely touched by that and moved by that experience. I had been there in a
previous life, actually. In fact, I was feeling slightly concerned when I heard Megan
Woods talk about all of her entertaining times at the Dux de Lux because I have had a
few times there myself, as part of a visiting University of Waikato sports team, and I
was wondering whether she might have even been at that bar at the very same time. I
cannot recall it, but perhaps that did occur. But it was a fantastic place then, and
obviously it is on quite an extraordinary journey of recovery.
The other point that has been made here this afternoon that I do want to acknowledge
is the extraordinary passion that the local people of Christchurch express when they talk
about the Arts Centre and the opportunity that is in front of the city to rebuild. I guess I
reflect, as a local MP from the Bay of Plenty, that obviously we do not have anything
like that in Tauranga. We have more natural icons. Mount Maunganui —Mauao—is an
example. I recall, when that was devastated by fire a few years ago, the incredible
emotional reaction that occurred in our local community. I guess I can put that in only a
small way to that same reaction. The people of Christchurch are hugely passionate about
what it represents, which is the heart of the city, and they are ensuring that that heritage
value is protected and rebuilt.
As we have heard earlier from Scott Simpson, our c hair, this is quite an investment
that is being undertaken here. It is 7 years’ effort and $300 million of expenditure, and I
do want to acknowledge Jen Crawford, the chair, and André Lovatt, the chief executive
officer, for their tireless commitment to work for the vision of rebuilding what is clearly
an extraordinary cultural heart. Their passion for and commitment to this is quite
extraordinary.
As you walk around that site—speaking as somebody who is not from the area —you
see the acute attention to det ail. Every single one of those crumbled stone pieces is
documented, it is put on a particular pallet, it is protected with wrap, and it is waiting
for its opportunity to be either rebuilt or used as an example so that a copy of it can be
rebuilt by the incredibly talented people who are there.
2824 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 1 Apr 2015
It was interesting to have just four submitters attending. I had thought that perhaps
something with this degree of community interest in it might well have had more, but it
was clear that the submitters spoke in lar ge alignment with each other, and they
certainly had a fair amount of support from the wider community.
I think it is a great bill to support. It is very good to see bills like this come to this
Chamber with cross -party support. It is sensible legislation and there is an opportunity
to progress something that is going to work for the community of Canterbury.
I do want to take a moment to reflect on one of the amendments that is required
under this change, and that is a move from a stakeholder -representative board to a skill-
based board. I think that is laudable. I think it is absolutely appropriate to be considered.
I think it was very appropriate that the community ensured that that change had broad
stakeholder support, and I note that the University of Ca nterbury, the Christchurch City
Council, Heritage New Zealand Pouhere Taonga, the Christchurch Civic Trust, and
Papatipu Rūnanga of Canterbury are examples of the stakeholders that have been
consulted.
I think it is very important, though, that that engag ement with the stakeholders does
not cease here. Clearly, there is now a significant power and influence that will be
passed to this new trust governance group. It is appropriate that a different mix of skills
is required to be able to take it forward for the next 10, 15, 20, or 30 years. But that trust
board must never forget from whence it has come in terms of the broad community
stakeholder engagement and the representation on the trust to date and in terms of what
is important to have still influencing the perspectives of that new skills-based board.
I do hope that the nominations that come forward for that board are appropriately
global in scope. I have no experience in arts council governance, but I have had some
experience in governance and senior management in previous roles before entering here.
We always, I think, have a bias to be very local, at times parochial, regional, and, at
best, national only in terms of the perspectives we bring to the table. For me it is really
important that the skill se ts that are sought to represent the community and this trust
board are as global as possible because, as we heard from some of the submitters, if you
have an objective to be able to promote not only the acknowledgment of good heritage
and phenomenal art and culture but also education, you need to make sure that the most
modern approaches of engaging with communities and making them feel part of their
history are adopted. Sometimes those best practices do not necessarily come from
within. You need to have more global representatives sitting around the table.
I do think it was very positive that the change agreed was that we would have the
conservation plan available at annual general meetings. I thought it was slightly
surprising, but perhaps reflective of a  more representative governance model, that that
conservation plan had not been reviewed for a number of years. I think the idea now of
having that available at every annual general meeting is going to drive a more frequent
refreshment of that plan. I think it is in many ways the soul, if you like, of the Arts
Centre of Christchurch Trust to ensure that that continues to be available to the public,
that it is updated as necessary, and that stakeholder engagement is part of it. I think it is
very important t hat this legislation does lock those objectives into legislation. It
provides, as the member Scott Simpson said, a security and stability for the community
going forward.
This is a really positive bill. It reflects a wide community endeavour. It is a very ,
very expensive community endeavour, but I am very sure that at the end of this, when
we finally get through to the third reading and we have the approval of this House, we
will have a platform provided for the community of Canterbury that will see it into the
future. Thank you.
1 Apr 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 2825

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. I am very pleased to
speak on behalf of the Green Party in support of the bill, and I join the chorus of
approval for the bi ll, promoted by the Hon Nicky Wagner. It certainly is not a
controversial bill. As others have noted, there were only four submissions and they were
generally supportive of the bill’s intent to provide a legislative basis for the trust’s work,
to update and modernise its governance, to consolidate its administration, and to enable
the trust to do the work on recovering the Arts Centre from the Canterbury earthquakes.
I am enormously grateful for the vision of those who successfully advocated in the
1970s to protect the Arts Centre buildings against demolition. That would have been a
travesty. I am also very grateful for the trust board because we have seen, as Ruth
Dyson noted, wholesale destruction of heritage buildings in Christchurch post the
quakes beca use of the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority’s casualness about
heritage and its keenness to use the section 38 notices under the emergency legislation
to sign off on the demolition of Cranmer Court, the Majestic Theatre, and over 200
other significant heritage buildings in the central city. The work being done by the trust
board on strengthening and repairing and restoring the Arts Centre is really significant
because of how much we have lost.
It is also significant because of the importance of the se buildings. There are 23
buildings on the Arts Centre site. All but one of them are listed as category 1 historic
places by Heritage New Zealand Pouhere Taonga. They are buildings with special or
outstanding historical or cultural heritage significance and value.
Like others, I pay tribute to the current Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Board, to
the leadership it is providing, to its chair Jen Crawford and the chief executive officer,
André Lovatt, and to the skill and dedication of all of those who are working on the site,
from the international team of stonemasons to the design engineers, the craftsman
carpenters, the plasterers, and the builders. All but one of these 23 buildings have
sustained significant damage, so we have a restoration project that is costing about $290
million and is going to take 7 years, and it is expected to be completed in 2019. When
you go behind the safety fences and have a look at the work that is being done, it is easy
to see that the challenges are immense. Buildings are being completely gutted. Floors
are being lifted. Timber ceilings are being peeled back to enable concrete cap beams to
be put in place. There is proper earthquake strengthening. A lot more attention to
modern technology will ensure that these buildings st ay warm. Having been a tenant of
the Old Chemistry Building, which was freezing in winter, that is a very welcome
addition.
This legislation is good legislation. The objects of the trust, in clause 5, are for the
Arts Centre to be held in trust as an outs tanding cultural centre for use by Christchurch
residents and visitors. The vision of the trust board and its staff is for the Arts Centre to
be a cultural hub of the city and region, a vibrant place of culture, art, and education. If
this bill can help ac hieve that aim, it will be very worthwhile. The Arts Centre
buildings, like the Canterbury Museum, and like Christchurch Cathedral, are neo-Gothic
buildings, which were popular in the Victorian era. They revive the details and forms of
the original Gothic style of the Middle Ages.
The Arts Centre was designed by using six different architectural practices. It was
built over about 50 years, but it has cohesion and unity. The architects have respected
the work of those who have gone before them. Two of the m ajor architects for the Arts
Centre were Benjamin Mountfort and Samuel Hurst -Seager. They were responsible for
the grand design of the precinct and features like the quadrangles. Benjamin Mountfort
also had a major role in the design of the Canterbury Muse um and the Christchurch
Cathedral. And, of course, these buildings are all linked by Worcester Street, now
Worcester Boulevard.
2826 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 1 Apr 2015
But there has been a very different approach between what has happened at the Arts
Centre and what is happening at the cathedral. The former Arts Centre trust board had
the wisdom to ensure that the Arts Centre was very well insured. That meant that the
restoration and strengthening work was able to start quickly, and it was assisted by
some generous local and international donati ons. At the Arts Centre we are seeing the
extraordinary challenges being responded to with inspiration and passion to develop
creative solutions to those engineering challenges. We have a lot of energy, a can -do
attitude, a pride in what is being done, and an obvious sign of progress with the rebuild.
It is an inspiring project.
Christchurch Cathedral is the very opposite. Because of the obduracy of the Church
Property Trustees and their failure to even protect the interior of the cathedral from the
weather by closing the gaping wound of what was once the rose window and the spires,
the whole cathedral has now become a symbol of failure. It is a symbol of having been
defeated by the earthquakes, and yet it could be so very different.
I strongly encourage the Bishop of Christchurch, Rt Rev. Victoria Matthews, and the
Church Property Trustees to do what the Local Government and Environment
Committee did and take a visit to the Arts Centre and see what can be achieved if you
have got passion, leadership, engineering skill, and commitment to restoring a place that
is important to the people of Christchurch. Eighty percent of the cathedral structure still
stands, the roof structure is entirely intact, and over 100 structural and seismic engineers
have said that there is no need to demolish it. They have said that the cathedral could be
restored and, with modern seismic strengthening, could comply with the highest code
standards for public buildings.
The Great Christchurch Buildings Trust has estimated that the co st of restoring the
cathedral would be around $67 million, substantially less than what it is costing to
restore the Arts Centre, and that trust has offered to help the Church Property Trustees
meet the $27 million shortfall between the church’s insurance payments and the cost of
restoration.
The building of the Christchurch Cathedral was a huge undertaking for a small
community; it took 40 years to complete. The Arts Centre restoration is taking 7 years
and the cathedral restoration may take a similar time. But given that these buildings
have been around for over a century and given that they will outlast us all, that is a very
short time. So I would encourage Bishop Matthews and the Church Property Trustees to
look at what real leadership, creative energy , and a respect for the craftsmanship and
skill of the past is doing at the Arts Centre and to look at what strong vision to return
and retain a cultural treasure is achieving, and then apply that to the cathedral. What has
been achieved at the Arts Centre has many practical lessons for restoring the cathedral.
The cathedral was designed by the same architect, Benjamin Mountfort. It has got
some of the same materials —those big basalt and limestone blocks, the big timber
supports and roof trusses, and the s late roof. The Christchurch Cathedral, like the Arts
Centre, is one of Christchurch’s landmarks, it is a legacy of our history, and it can be a
symbol of the city again, but there needs to be a major change in attitude by the Church
Property Trustees and by the bishop. It needs them to be inspired by the same vision and
sense of purpose that we are seeing in the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Board,
which this bill is designed to encourage. Thank you. The Green Party is very pleased to
support this bill.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to likewise endorse
and signal that we will be supporting the passage of the Arts Centre of Christchurch
Trust Bill, not just through this reading but through to the conclusion. I am going to
pick up on some of the themes of some of the speeches before me. It is very hard when
you get a bill that is quite simple, you come in as speaker No. 7, and pretty much
1 Apr 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 2827
everything that can be said about the Arts C entre has been said. So I am going to pick
up on a couple of comments. I am going to pick up on something as a former Mayor of
Carterton—the comments about the former Local Government and Environment

items.speaker: Committee. I do need to say this
items.text: the previous select committee was not viewed on very
well by local government in general. I am pleased that I am working—

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: Maybe it was that mayor.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: —on a select committee—there is chipping in from some young man
over there; I will get his name soon. It will come back to me.

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: Old age is setting in.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: Oh, yap, yap, yap. Do I need to talk about Northland to shut that
member up? I probably could, but I will move on. This select committee seems to have
a very nice culture—and it is interesting that we are talking about arts and culture at this
time—within it. I am pleased to be sitting on a committee that has a high degree of
cohesion and collegiality about it. I have to say, though, that when I look back over my
career in Parliament, some select committees have not had that air, that culture, about
them. The previous Local  Government and Environment Committee earned itself a
reputation in local government for being pretty pigheaded and bloody -minded,
particularly from the Government’s side. That was not evident today. It is not evident
under the chairmanship of Scott Simpson—

items.speaker: Hon Nicky Wagner
items.text: I would start being very worried about a strike.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: —and I am happy to say that I am looking forward to continuing
working in the same vein as we progress through. It is not hard. If you want to hear
those messages, go talk to any mayor about the way in which the previous Local
Government and Environment Committee heard their submissions on the amalgamation
proposals and on the changes to the Local Government Act. They were quite disgusted
and appalled by the body language and behaviour of some of the members, Nicky —
quite disgusted, actually, but moving forward.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Not by all parties, surely.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: No, no, not by all parties. One party thought that that behaviour was
quite appropriate and that was the National Party.
There were comments about Margaret Austin —and the Hon Margaret Austin has
been the chair of the trust board—and it really does give me great pleasure to hear those
comments about Margaret, because in  her time both in Parliament and in Christchurch
she has done sterling work across the community, and this is just another fine example
of it.
Looking at the history of the trust, I note that the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust
Board was established in 1978. That was 4 years after I arrived in Christchurch from the
North Island as a young soldier. I can say that from then, 1974, until when I left
Christchurch in 2007, the transformation in the Arts Centre was absolutely astonishing.
It went from being a place that had huge, obvious historic and cultural value to being a
place that had all the signs of falling into disrepair and even dereliction. But because of
the efforts of a lot of very talented and committed Cantabrians over those years from
1978 to 2007, I saw it transformed as it was renovated, revived, and energised into
becoming a vibrant centre of entertainment, art, education, and trade. It became a centre
of entertainment not just for Cantabrians but for people who visited Christchurch. I can
say that as I grew and eventually became a family man with children, I absolutely
adored any opportunity to take my kids into the Arts Centre and to enjoy the
entertainment and enjoy the arts and the cultures that were exhibited there so often. I
think 1.5 mi llion people —the records state here —were going through, visiting there
every year. Even those figures quite astonished me when I read them recently.
2828 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 1 Apr 2015
I have spoken to many people all over the South Island who have had the opportunity
to visit the Arts Centr e. It would be fair to say that their views and their experiences of
the Arts Centre are pretty similar to those that have been expressed in the House here
today. Of course, one could not get through this debate without mentioning the Dux de
Lux. I see that the honourable member Megan Woods mentioned that, and Todd Muller.
Obviously, a number of university students partook in that little place, and I can say that
a number of soldiers from Burnham Military Camp who partook in there on the odd
occasion have always enjoyed the Dux de Lux and have enjoyed that opportunity to mix
with people whom we probably would not meet socially on a normal basis, particularly
those of us in the military. Artistically, culturally, historically, the Christchurch Arts
Centre epi tomised Christchurch and Christchurch people. It epitomised, clearly, their
heritage and their culture, but in many, many ways it also epitomised their innovation
and their determination not to allow a taonga that was so important to them to fall into a
state of disrepair or, even worse, disappear.
Of course, we all know that in 2010 and 2011 Christchurch was hit by those rather
devastating earthquakes. Again, I am someone who considers himself to be a
Cantabrian by 30 years’ occupation, even though I am f rom the Wairarapa, and my
family were down there. I was fortunate —and unfortunate—in having family members
who were in the Fire Service, family members who were in urban search and rescue,
and family members who were in the police. I was fortunate to get a  very unique
opportunity to visit the red zone and view the devastation in places like the Arts Centre
firsthand at a very early stage when most other New Zealanders were locked out of the
place. It was a privilege that I still treasure, and I know it was not one that was afforded
to other people.
Looking at the level of damage and having an engineering background myself, I
could only shake my head and wonder how the heck some of this work was ever going
to be completed, and whether there was ever going to be a full restoration. I understand
the angst and the heartache from people who lament the decisions made around the
cathedral. Anyone who has lived in Christchurch for 30 years on and off understands
how important the English heritage and the English cult ure—and particularly the
cathedral—is to Cantabrians. This particular project was always going to be extremely
demanding for those who were entrusted with the responsibility of rebuilding, restoring,
and conserving the Arts Centre going forward.
This bill, brought in by Nicky Wagner —and I congratulate the honourable
member—seeks to address some of the impediments that were inherent in the former
governance model. Having returned to Parliament and seen this bill, which came in last
year, I can, and New Zeal and First can, understand and concur with the honourable
member Nicky Wagner that change was necessary if the good people of Christchurch
were to do the task that was confronting them. Modernising the governance structure,
affirming the responsibility of ownership and duty to it, removing the political influence
that comes with ministerial and political party -  influenced appointments—and it does
not matter whether it is a red -dominated Government or a blue -dominated
Government—are never actually going to d eliver to you all of the skill sets that one
requires in this task ahead.

items.speaker: Hon Jo Goodhew
items.text: What about yourself?

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: I know. I brought wonderful skill sets and your former Minister Tony
Ryall absolutely acknowledged it, and I am grateful for that recognition. But the
member herself knows from her time in Opposition that one can look at some
ministerial appointments and  think that, given the challenges of a $290 million project
to be conducted over 7 years, the skill sets in this case need to be very defined. So the
1 Apr 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 2829
amendments here to address that are very good amendments, and we support them
wholeheartedly.
We would sa y, I guess, that culture is something that some of us look at with
different eyes. I look at some of the things that were lost in Christchurch, and we lament
those losses. Let us just hope that looking back at the Christchurch Arts Centre in 7 or 8
years f rom now —and at the new board of trustees as they have undertaken their full
restoration and rebuild work, working and focusing on conservation—we will be proud
that we supported that effort here this afternoon. Thank you.

items.speaker: PAUL FOSTER-BELL
items.text: Tēnā koe e te Mana Whakawā. I rise to speak
on behalf of the Government in the second reading debate on the Arts Centre of
Christchurch Trust Bill. Far be it from me to correct the honourable membe r Dr Megan
Woods, but I did just want to raise one small issue. In her speech she described this bill
as a local bill. Of course, it is important to recognise that this is in fact a private bill.
A private bill is something that, although not abhorrent to this House, is relatively
rare because, in general, as a constitutional principle, we prefer to pass general
legislation that has equal effect for all. However, I actually agree with previous speakers
in this debate that such is the value of the Christchurch Arts Centre, not only to
Christchurch but to New Zealand, and even in a global context, that this bill is
appropriate. It is appropriate that we put in place specific, enabling legislation to
enshrine the objects and powers of the trust and its board, and to protect this asset,
which is of enormous value to the people of Canterbury and to the citizens of New
Zealand.
I had, I suppose, the pleasure of training as an archaeologist at the University of
Otago. I bring this up for a couple of reasons. Firstly, I am not entirely unaware of some
of the issues around heritage management and rehabilitating dilapidated old ruins,
having spent several years during my university time with a trowel, brush, and shovel in
such sites. Secondly, because the University of Otago, like the Arts Centre, is in that
wonderful neo -Gothic style —in fact, the Christchurch Arts Centre is described as
collegiate, or collegial, Gothic it is, as the very distinguished and discerning member
Scott Simpson pointed out, built to emulate t he mores of Victorian Britain. But it is
actually unique in the world as a consolidated example of that style of architecture in a
precinct—not just in individual buildings but consistent across entire city blocks—and it
is something that is very precious to us. In fact, prior to the devastating earthquakes, the
Arts Centre precinct, along with the Christchurch Cathedral, was being considered for
recognition and for World Heritage status to be inscribed to it on the World Heritage
List by Unesco because of its unique nature and its value, not only for New Zealand but
globally. So this is a timely bill.
It is important that after 30 or 40 years of operation, we modernise some provisions
that govern the original trust. I think we should also note the excellen t work that is
being done by the existing trust board and the good management of the staff, led by
André Lovatt as chief executive officer of the Arts Centre. They are in a strong position
due to that good management. After the devastating first earthquake  in 2010, which did
a lot of physical damage —a lot less human damage, death, and destruction was
wreaked—the Christchurch Arts Centre very sensibly reinsured. It settled quickly and
reinsured.
So the reason we now have one of the largest —in fact, the largest, as Scott Simpson
said—heritage restoration projects currently under way in the world is that the Arts
Centre was sensible in its approach to insurance and managed to secure a nearly $300
million payout from insurers to enable it to undertake that 7- year restoration process.
The additional funding, of course, being applied by the Government does help, but in a
situation where we are inevitably forced to prioritise and juggle between hospitals,
2830 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 1 Apr 2015
schools, arts precincts, and other buildings it is useful to have significant money coming
in from insurance providers.
I do not have the connections to Canterbury that some other members have, but I do
have a fondness for the Arts Centre building. I enjoyed David McPhail’s play Muldoon,
performed in the Court The atre. It would have been about 10 years ago, in the early
2000s. Having visited, along with colleagues from the Local Government and
Environment Committee, to have a look at the work that is being done there, it was
very, very clear not only that is there high quality in terms of the management of the
organisation but that it really is a “United Nations of restoration”. You hear Irish
accents. You see people from the Czech Republic, those from the UK, those from
Europe, those from Asia—from all around the world—contributing to maintaining some
of these crafts and trades that have been lost over the years, but are now being re -
inculcated and retaught. So we have not only plasterers and stonemasons but also
people who work in wood and people who are experts in the electrical wiring of
heritage buildings, to avoid the unfortunate risk of fire, which you get when you have
these buildings where certain fundaments cannot be changed.
This is a good piece of legislation. The objects of this legislation are not for t he
Government to step in and determine on behalf of the people of Canterbury how the
centre should be managed. In fact, it is quite the opposite. This bill enshrines a role for
the trust board that includes holding the trust property for the objects that have been laid
out. These objects are to hold and develop the Arts Centre as a unique and outstanding
