cultural centre for use by the people of Christchurch, and—equally important in my
view—to foster, promote, and facilitate an interest and involvement in t he arts, culture,
creativity, the creative industries, and educational purposes.
We saw this in play when we visited the Arts Centre site and it was explained to us
that in previous incarnations the buildings were used for such features as cafes and art
galleries. Of course, there will be those facilities in the restored Arts Centre. But we
were also shown the fact that they will have state -of-the-art laboratories, including 3D
printing—this new technology that allows something to be designed on a computer  and
then realised in plastic or polymer form almost instantaneously. This is very expensive
equipment, but it will take the arts that are developed there to a new level. It is very
appropriate for this modern age in which we live.
The powers of the trust  board as enshrined in this bill are fairly far -reaching. In fact,
they have the full capacity to carry on or undertake any activity that advances the
objects of the Arts Centre. That includes the acquisition of further real or personal
property of any nat ure that may be useful for the maintenance of the Arts Centre, and
being able to let, or lease, the lands and buildings so that the buildings can be let out and
put to use, because, as we know, when heritage buildings are engaged in a useful
purpose, they are more likely to be valued and respected but also maintained. The trust
board is allowed to construct, re-erect, improve, maintain, and provide further buildings,
and, of course, that is important in a situation where we are in the middle of a major
restoration project.
The trust board will be empowered to employ staff —an important factor also in
terms of managing such a significant site. It will be able to borrow money. It will have
the ability to make a business decision as to whether it needs to seek a mortgage or
debenture or some sort of injection of capital to enable the board to achieve its aims —
although, of course, as I have mentioned, that $300 million insurance payment does
help significantly towards the reconstruction —and it is able to generate public
subscriptions and donations. So it is able to do a wide range of things. This is not a bill
that is about the Government putting more power in its own hands. In fact, this is a bill
1 Apr 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 2831
that modernises the settings for the Arts Centre of Christchurch T rust Board and
actually empowers it to deliver.
I do want to raise a few other points. I congratulate the Minister, the Hon Nicky
Wagner, who has demonstrated, I think, with the excellent majority with which she held
the seat of Christchurch Central at th e last election that she is an incredibly hard -
working MP and that she has been a passionate and tireless advocate for this project in
particular.
I would like to acknowledge the chair of the Local Government and Environment
Committee and all of our colle agues. Given the comments from Mr Mark I would have
to agree with his description of the committee as being a group of people who have an
interest in working together collegially—which is appropriate when we are dealing with
collegial Gothic buildings—and who take a sophisticated and, I think, quite enlightened
approach to dealing with this issue and making sure that the right things are done.
The committee did suggest a number of amendments to the bill. There probably is
not time to go through each and every one of those today. But I think, in a general
sense, that it is important that we achieve a position where people are on the trust board
due to the skill set they bring rather than because they represent specific interest groups
in society. We need p eople who have accounting knowledge, legal knowledge,
Government expertise, and, importantly, heritage management expertise on the
governance body for the Arts Centre so that it can be run well into the future. Thank
you very much.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call is a split call. Jan
Logie—5 minutes.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: It is with pleasure that I rise to speak on this, the second
reading of the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill, a private bill brought to this
House by the Hon Nicky Wagner. I would like to commend the Associate Minister for
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery on the smooth progress of this bill so far through the
House, and also for the demonstration that is within this bill of a connection to
community and a valuing of heritage, and the importance that that plays within
Christchurch. We do see that evident in this bill. I guess it is just a shame that that
connection to community and that valuing of heritage have run up against the
immovable force of the Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery and the wider
National caucus. This has meant we have not seen those same values being able to be
applied in a wider sense in Christchurch.
The Arts Centre building —it has been interesting listening in the House tonight to
how many people from Christchurch have spoken so passionately about this place. I too
have a link to Christchurch in that my mother was very proud to have adopted
Canterbury for herself. She has the Crusaders theme song on her phone and is very
passionate about this city now. I have visited her there many times and spent time at the
Arts Centre. We have been to plays there. We have seen movies there. We have be en to
the art gallery there. We have had coffee there. We have been shopping there. I think it
just speaks to what a hub this place is in its essence as well as in carrying so many
stories, which we have heard mentioned in other members’ speeches tonight, around the
famous people —Rutherford—who were there, the meaning that is held within those
buildings, and the traditions as well as just everyday experiences of locals on a daily
basis that are held in those buildings. They are very special for the people of
Christchurch and for those of us who are not Cantabrians but have links to that place.
The Arts Centre is a massive drawcard for so many foreign visitors. You see the
tourists walking up and down those avenues, just being drawn to that place because it is
such a special place. It is wonderful to have the opportunity to speak on behalf of the
preservation of that and the protection of those values and that tradition within
2832 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 1 Apr 2015
Christchurch, particularly—and I do have to mention it again—in the face of so much
devastation within the central city of Christchurch. Enabled by section 38 of the
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Act, there have been 1,240 demolitions within those
four avenues, and 20 percent of those were heritage buildings.
The Majestic Centre—again, there are the things I have been to there and the stories
that those walls have held for the generations of people who settled in Christchurch.
There is also Cranmer Court. These heritage buildings are not just old dungers, as
described by the Minister fo r Canterbury Earthquake Recovery. They are holders of
love, tradition, and meaning for the people of Christchurch, and it has been such a loss
to see so much of that taken away for wider roads —for some enforced vision created in
the head of a Minister sitting most of his time in Wellington. So it is so welcome to
have the opportunity to be part of something that protects a section of what was —to
enable those traditions and those memories to carry on into the future and into the future
well beyond us in this House.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Jacinda Ardern—5 minutes.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I think it has been quite uplifting to hear  members
across the House talk with such passion about the importance of protecting important
historic and heritage buildings in New Zealand and specifically within the Christchurch
context. I think that is incredibly important, given the loss that that city and that region
have experienced in terms of their heritage buildings. I do want to come back to that in a
little bit.
Speaking directly to the Arts Centre though, I too, like many other members across
this House, visited the centre both before and pos t - the quakes. Post - the quakes I was
left with absolutely no doubt about the passion that is held by those who are working on
this project for doing the very best job they can on behalf of the people of Canterbury to
preserve such an important cluster o f buildings. There are, however, a few issues that
relate to the Arts Centre. Obviously, it was the home of the University of Canterbury for
more than a century. It comprises 23 heritage buildings. They are collectively registered
as category I historic places under the Heritage New Zealand Pouhere Taonga Act, and,
of course, with such a significant number of buildings it is a large project —it is 7 years
and it is $290 million.
The definition around the buildings that has been used struck a little bit of
controversy, though, at the select committee. To be fair, very few things, I think, did
raise any question marks. But two of the submissions did raise concerns about
references in the bill to “historic stone buildings”, which, of course, is the majority  of
the buildings, I understand, but that does leave out, as currently drafted, protections for
the former student union building, which would be known to many as Dux de Lux, and
it has been referred to in a number of speeches in this House. Although I understand that
the issue over the protections not relating to that building has been raised with those
who are members of the Arts Centre trust, they have said that the plans are not really
locked in for that building, as I understand it, as has been reported, a nd that there is still
a longer-term plan around that building that needs to be developed.
Given that this particular part of the centre’s grounds has not been included in the
definition, I think it would be helpful if the trust were able to give words of comfort,
particularly to those from Historic Places Canterbury who have spoken out about this
issue and are really seeking assurances that it is part of the wider plan. Even though it is
not included in the definition, by virtue of being a brick and wood building as opposed
to being a stone building, I think there is room for the trust to work collaboratively with
those advocates who are trying to ensure that that building is looked after too. That is
just one of the points that I wanted to make.
1 Apr 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 2833
I do also want to just touch on the fact that provision has been made in the bill for
legacy around the trust. If the trust is wound up, the trust property would be vested in
the Crown. I think that is a really important part of the bill. Of course we would hope
that we would not have a set of circumstances that would allow that, but I have seen
cases in the past where there has not been proper provision for that, and it has led to
disastrous results.
Speaking of disastrous results, I want to spend only a quick par t of my contribution
on the wider issues around heritage buildings in Canterbury. There have been 1,240
demolitions as of February 2015 within the four avenues, compared with 292 rebuild
consents, and 20 percent of those demolitions have been of heritage buildings. The
centre of Christchurch has lost 50 percent of its heritage buildings, and often that
happened with great haste and, in some cases, without it being necessary. The Majestic
Theatre is a prime example of that. Labour, almost a year ago to the day, called for
section 38 of the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Act to no longer be applied to
heritage buildings, to give proper Resource Management Act process to the removal of
heritage buildings. Yes, safety was a very necessary concern in the beginnin g, but that
moment has moved on and we were seeing, time and time again, decisions of
expediency at the cost of heritage. I would hope that there is an end to that process now
in Christchurch.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: Tēnā koe e te Mana Whakawā. I am pleased to stand
to speak on the second reading of the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill, but before
I get going I just want to give some clarification. This Government is —is—concerned
about the rebuild of Christchurch, and $15 billion - plus is not exactly a little drop in the
bucket. We are caring about what is happening with the Christchurch rebuild; it is one
of our major priority areas. I just wanted to put that out there in response to what was
said by a previous speaker from the Green Party. I also want to say that I moved to
Christchurch East just before the by -election—it would have been about June of last
year—and found my whakapapa roots there. I am one of the mokopuna of Tahu Pōtiki ,
whose older brother is Porourangi. Porourangi is my direct ancestor, through my father
and Ngati Porou. I just wanted to put that there.
As I move into my speech, I want to thank the Hon Nicky Wagner for bringing this
bill to the House. It is a very good bill, a nd I am really pleased that it has cross -party
support. The Arts Centre is one of the most significant clusters of heritage buildings in
New Zealand. It is a cultural asset, not only just locally but nationally and
internationally as well. I know that the people of Christchurch love their Arts Centre.
Maybe I was too young to go to the Dux de Lux —I do not know. I did not know much
about that place, but anyway, from all accounts, I can see that many people did enjoy
what the Dux de Lux offered up. Again, I a m carrying on with thanking Nicky for
bringing this bill to the House. I am also going to thank Scott Simpson, as the chair of
our Local Government and Environment Committee. I was one of the members of the
Justice and Electoral Committee last year, and be ing a new MP it was really good to be
under his chairmanship. He chairs the meetings very well and collegially. The Local
Government and Environment Committee is not the only one he has chaired; he has also
chaired the Justice and Electoral Committee, and I thank you, Scott, for your wise
counsel and for your leadership in that select committee.
As I move on to the Arts Centre, as I said, the Arts Centre is a historic building. As
Eugenie Sage said, it reflects the distinct architectural designs of Benjami n Woolfield
Mountfort, and it also, as I said, reflects the history of local education, with a strong
connection, obviously, to arts and science. Its main pupil, or student, was Ernest, Lord
Rutherford. He completed his undergraduate degree there, at Cante rbury College, as
2834 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 1 Apr 2015
well as most of his breakthrough research. So it has got a special place in the hearts of
everybody who has used it.
The Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Board, which is the group that governs the
Arts Centre, was established in December 1978 and incorporated under the Charitable
Trusts Act of 1957. My colleagues have already outlined the devastating 2010 and 2011
earthquakes that hit Christchurch, leaving 22 of the 23 buildings in dire need of repair.
That repair is going to be a 7 -year and a near -on $300 million restoration programme,
which is currently under way. As many have heard, the Local Government and
Environment Committee met there a few months ago. We were privileged to go through
the Arts Centre. I was unable to go there —I had worn the wrong shoes—so I will enjoy
heading back to Christchurch to have a bit of a look through the building and see its
progress thus far. As I said before, it is the largest heritage restoration building, not only
here, but currently in the world. It is a significant milestone for New Zealand to have
that project ongoing. Not only does it provide back to the people of Christchurch their
beloved Arts Centre but it also sits within the world records, and because it is there, it is
basically a flagstone f or international visitors to come and visit this wonderful centre
once it is completed.
I just want to talk a little bit about the trust board and some of the impacts that the
earthquakes have had on it. With the impact of the earthquakes, there have to be some
changes or some adaptations within the trust board. Some of my colleagues have
already talked about the skills -based board appointments. They have an appointments
committee with which to do that. I want to acknowledge André Lovatt, the chief
executive officer, and Jen Crawford, the chair of the trust board, for the work that they
have been doing —and the work that lies ahead of them, based on some of the clauses
within this bill.
I want to move to some of the new provisions, some of the key changes s et out in
schedule 2, which looks at the constitution of the trust board with some of the key
changes. Some of the areas that I want to talk about are the new provisions in clauses 1
to 4 of schedule 2. These deal with trust board membership and look at the number of
board appointments. Seven to nine members can be appointed to the board. As I
mentioned earlier, there is an appointments committee that has been set up. Some of my
colleagues have also discussed vacancies on the board, which may arise from tim e to
time. Some of the key stakeholders such as the University of Canterbury, the
Christchurch City Council, Heritage New Zealand Pouhere Taonga, the Christchurch
Civic Trust, the Papatipu Rūnanga  of Canterbury—which I am sure my colleague Nuk
will talk a little bit more in depth about—other such local businesses and community
organisations, and the Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage will have an interest in
vacancies and in the Arts Centre as it progresses. This area of clauses 1 to 4 also talks
about how vacancies will be made available. That will be done through the chief
executive officer publicly advertising the vacancies in the local newspapers and various
other areas.
I want to talk a little bit now about the revised provisions relating to the pr oceedings
of the trust board, which is in clause 5 of schedule 2. This looks at a new requirement
for the board to hold an annual public meeting where the conservation plan will be
placed for input and all viewing, and, as amended, it also talks about what  the quorum
will be, as well about voting.
We have talked a little about the revised provisions dealing with the accounts of the
trust board and other areas. I just want to talk a little bit about clause 10(a) of schedule
2, which deals with the protection of board members from liability. That is really key,
because when you ask people to come on to boards and help to govern particular
organisations, especially this one —it is a very key one for the community —we want to
1 Apr 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 2835
be able to protect them, and so claus e 10(a) puts in the ability for board members to be
protected from liability for loss to the trust.
Finally, clauses 10(b) and (c) look at indemnity. I am going to read this. New clause
10(b) provides that “Each board member [may] be indemnified by the tr ust against all
actions, proceedings, claims, damages, losses, demands, costs (including legal costs),
and expenses suffered by or incurred by that member in connection with the trust .” That
is really key, because when you start advertising for new board m embers, those are
some of the things that they will be looking at —especially those from a skills -based
background, because they are professionals. They bring in their professional
backgrounds or their community links, and they want to know that they are going to be
safe within the board where they are representing their community.
In closing, we are going to pay them. Clause 11 of schedule 2 looks at providing for
the remuneration of board members, and it is nice to be able to give them something in
recognition of the skills that they bring to their role as trust board members of the
Christchurch Arts Centre. Again, I am very proud to be standing and speaking on behalf
of the Government supporting the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill. Kia ora.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: Meitaki maata, Mr Assistant
Speaker, and thank you for the opportunity to speak on the Arts Centre of Christchurch
Trust Bill. Firstly, my acknowledgments go to the Hon Nicky Wagner for guiding this
bill in its passage through the House. There is widespread support for what this bill aims
to do. I also need to acknowledge Jen Crawford and André Lovatt from the trust board
itself. Further, I want to acknowledge the Hon Margaret Austin, who is a former Labour
member and someone whom the Christchurch community owes a great debt of gratitude
for her desire to ensure that our city and our province recovers well.
The trust board has worked tirelessly, and it is an extraordinary piece of legislation in
that the board’s trust deeds and objects, the powers under which it will wo rk, and all the
provisions that provide for the trust board are enshrined in legislation. It is not the
normal way you would do things, but it is a very significant and important step to
ensure that the work that is done to restore the buildings on that si te goes ahead. So I
acknowledge and support the aims of the trust board.

items.speaker: This legislation has three main aims
items.text: to create the legal framework in which the work
can be conducted, to amend the governance structure to ensure that the right people with
the right skills at the right time are in a position to ensure that this work is carried out,
and—the last aim—to enable and to respond to the recovery work that is required post
the earthquakes. The legislation  is significant. W e have heard other members in this
House speak this evening about what the centre means to them , and not just the centre
but the general precinct and the area that suffered significant damage. We are talking
not just about buildings and land; we are talking about areas where people and fam ilies
congregated and shared time together. Each one of those stones within the Arts Centre
building, each piece of wood, each window, and each area of courtyard and pavement
has a memory. The memories are of times that were spent there by students —happy
times; perhaps stressful times too, if you were a student and trying to get through
exams. There is more to this precinct than just the bricks and the stone. It is significant
that we acknowledge that that is part of the recovery and restoration process.
Other members have talked about the trust being set up in 1978, and my colleague Dr
Megan Woods talked about how that came to p ass in the early 1970s. I want to talk a
little bit about the objects of the trust  because this piece of legislation enshrines those.
The objects really are ensuring that we hold and develop the Arts Centre—the site, the
buildings—in trust as a unique and outstanding cultural centre for use by the people of
Christchurch and its visitors. I know that before moving to Christchurch to l ive, when I
was visiting family in Christchurch, it would always be one of the places we went to
2836 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 1 Apr 2015
because it always had the best coffee, and the market at  the weekend was a great place
to pick up knick- knacks. It was extraordinary to be able to watch the ar tisans at work
there using crafts from a past time.
One of the other objects is fostering, promoting, and facilitating interest and
involvement in art, culture, creativity, the creative industries, and education. There was
no cooler place to go than the Arts Centre if you were going to see a play, to hear music,
or to really just generally share in culture.
This bill also enshrines the powers of the trust, which include having the capacity to
ensure that any activity that the trust board deems necessary is able to be carried out and
that at any time that it needs to acquire property, even to demo lish buildings, or make
changes or employ staff, all of those activities are within this legislation. The legislation
is unable to be changed except so that the w ork of the trust board can go on as it needs
to through the period—through to 2019.
Further, there are two main parts to the bill. The first sets out its purpose and its
definitions around the committee and the trust deed. Those provisions describe the
schedules, which provide the detail of the land and the buildings within the bill. Part 2
sets out the objects of the trust, and the bill concludes with the schedules, which
describe the land and the constitution of the trust board.
Any discussion regarding  heritage buildings in Christchurch cannot be held without
thinking about section 38 of the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Act 2011 and the loss
of heritage to the city. The reason I refer to that in the context of other comments is that
I know that over t he last few summers, as the fences have started to come down in the
central city , as people have been able to go back into the  city, and as some of the
rebuilding work has been carried out, many people were reluctant to return because they
did not want to see the devastation that was there. It has been a re- traumatising of our
population, I guess, in a sense, to go back into the city and see just what needs to be
done and just what has been lost. I ask the Government to think long and hard about
whether we properly used section 38 when we were considering the demolition of many
of those heritage buildings.
My colleague Eugenie Sage also referred to the cathedral. When I talk about the
cathedral and when I talk about the significant heritage buildings in Chr istchurch, I
liken them to when we discuss our whakapapa and our pepeha . The maunga within it—
for those of us who do not have a connection to that part of the world in terms of our
cultural heritage—that we can refer to  are those buildings, the cat hedral a nd the Arts
Centre, and the significant beauty that our heritage buildings brought to the area.
Many of my colleagues have talked about the number of buildings that were lost
within the four avenues  area. Twenty  percent were our heritage buildings. That  is
significant. In order for recovery to occur to the fullest extent, we must acknowledge
what we have lost and what has pa ssed and ensure that we do not lose any more. So I
commend this bill to the House , and I encourage the Government to consider carefull y
the recovery of Christchurch. The recovery has not been completed. There are still
many areas where people are wanting this Government to step up. I cannot go past the
eastern suburbs in that comment, of course, where we are still to have our horizontal
infrastructure completed so we  can be fully recovered. So thank you to the Hon Nicky
Wagner. It is a great bill. Thank you.

The reflection of this bill here, and particularly the way that everyone has worked

The important thing too is to acknowledge my other colleagues, our MPs from the

that this had on tangata whenua—I am not talking about just the earthquake, because we
all suffered there. If we go back before that, with the arrival of the Europeans, what is
interesting with this building is that when we were young kids coming to Christchurch
from Tuahuriri in the northern part of the city, this particular building we saw as an
edifice to colonialism, so we never visited it much. We were on our way as schoolkids
to the museum to see our wonderful Māori artefacts that were inside there.
What I am saying here is that this particular building, when you look at the history of
the city and all of that, it really does actually now strike a chord with us in the fact that
it is part of us because of the fact of what went on during the earthquake, the rū whenua,
particularly in 2011.
What I am saying here, with this particular building, with everything that has gone
on, again, is that reflection that we are working together, particularly when you look at
the trust deed. The idea behind the resurrection of this building is pretty much w hen we
talk about a phoenix rising from the rubble. We have great opportunities during the
rebuild to not only rebuild our buildings but also to put in new ideas and to instil new
parts of the way we actually manage and govern these buildings.
This, again, is a reflection of the fact that we have re- established a legal foundation
for the Arts Centre in Christchurch in statute but also the reforms here that this bill is
doing. It reforms the governance arrangements by establishing a higher skills base. The
important thing there too is the fact of why we actually now believe —the member of
Parliament for Christchurch East referred to these buildings as taonga maunga, or

mauka. I would not go that far. I think that when you look at that, when you relate to
your mauka, it is Maukatere in North Canterbury, and when you look at your awa, it is
the Ōtākaro or the Ōpāwaho.
If you come down from that esoteric look at the spirituality and all of that, it is very
much around the natural landscape. But I do concur with the member about the fact of
the mana that this building does instil in all of us now, more so because it survived, in
some ways, the Christchurch earthquake. And we are all working together now to be
able to rebuild it back to a more significant and a more well-managed building.
When looking at the make -up of the new governance board, I think the important
thing is to look at the representation of the iwi, particularly because of the fact that we

representative there. And if we look at the way that it is governed, it is a fact that we can
actually instil—

Just to finish off, I was just finishing around the tangata whenua and also the

1 Apr 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 2839
CHRISTCHURCH CITY COUNCIL (RATES VALIDATION) BILL
Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I move, That the
Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill be now read a second time . As the
member in charge of the Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill, I really
welcome this second reading. This is a very simple bill. It is all about fixing an error, an
error that I believe was made with the best intentions. It is o ne of those really annoying
and frustrating situations where bad things happen when you are trying to do good. It is
about validating rates irregularities in the past that were only discovered by the city
council last year.
Back in 2004 the Christchurch C ity Council consciously opted to simplify the
language of its rating resolution, but it left out important information, which meant that
its resolution did not comply with the Local Government (Rating) Act 2002. All the
information that was required was pr esented, but it was presented elsewhere, and not in
the new simplified, streamlined resolution. On discovering that, the council undertook a
review of all its resolutions since 2004, and found other technical irregularities in
relation to seven targeted ra tes and the uniform annual general charge. Again, all the
correct information was provided, but not in the actual resolution. The council was able
to fix the mistakes for the 2013 and 2014 financial years, but it needs this validation bill
to validate its past setting of rates, payment dates, and penalty regimes. But let me make
this very clear: this is not about the rates being calculated wrongly, and all the rates
have been lawfully paid. No one is wrongfully affected by this bill.
I would like to thank the Local Government and Environment Committee for its
work in scrutinising this bill, for its support of the bill, and for the fact that it returned
this bill to the House unamended. I would also like to applaud the Christchurch City
Council for acting sw iftly to deal with this matter once it was discovered. Parliament
does not like validation bills. We hate the fact that we are dealing with retrospective
legislation. I am sure many members tonight will show their displeasure. But I have a
sympathy for the  council, because we also want simple legislation, we want simple
resolutions, and we want people to be able to understand what is going on in local
government. Also, nobody likes to admit that they have made a mistake, particularly if
it was well intentioned. There is always a temptation to let sleeping dogs lie, but the city
council has fronted up, and I say well done to it.
Actually, I would like to take this time to spend a few moments paying tribute to the
Christchurch City Council and updating the House on the huge workload it has had and
what it has been doing since the 2010 and 2011 earthquakes. As you all know, it has
been a tough time in Christchurch. It has been extremely difficult for the Christchurch
City Council to keep the business -as-usual work under control, as well as managing the
challenges of the rebuild. Everyone in Christchurch is aware that we have to fix the past
while we live in the present and while we build for the future, and that takes a bit of
juggling. We have learnt that out of crisis comes opportunity. We also feel that the only
way that we can reconcile the pain and loss of the last few years is by making sure we
take every opportunity to build a better place for future generations. The earthquakes
have sharpened our focus on what is important to the people in Christchurch.
Everyone in the council, and, actually, everyone who works in the Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery Authority, is absolutely committed to making Christchurch a safe,
beautiful, and people -friendly city. We want it to be a future -focused place, a place
where exciting, innovative, and enterprising things can happen. We want to retain our
sense of community and of supporting each other that served us so well during the
disaster, and also our open- mindedness and our action orientation that our shaken- up
2840 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 1 Apr 2015
city required, and our ability to work together for the greater good. Leading a
community in times of crisis and enormous change requires really tough decision-
making. Decisions have to be made rapidly, often with s cant information, in a changing
environment, and with a risk of unknown consequences. I pay tribute to the mayor,
Lianne Dalziel, and all the councillors and the officials who work at the Christchurch
City Council, for stepping up to that challenge and giving it their very best. I know at
times it feels a bit like a thankless task, but it is hugely important for the future of our
city, and their work is greatly appreciated by those who understand the challenges.
It has been over 140 years since Christchurch was first planned and built. Those were
the days of horses and carts, cooking on a fire or a wood stove, washing in the copper,
candles, and the dunny in the backyard. School was about slates and the strap, and life
was short. Today we are envisaging the  building of a modern, flexible, future -focused
city: a city of electric or even driverless cars, organic food and nutraceuticals; a city
with an integrated alternative energy grid, buildings that are automatically lit and heat-
adjusted, and with high- tech water and sewer schemes. School is an amazing modern
learning environment with digital devices, and our life expectancy is increasing year by
year. It is the responsibility of all of us to build a city that enables our community to
adapt and develop as ti mes change, and with the flexibility to be able to manage those
unknown innovations of the next 140 years.
In this bill, we validate unintentional errors in the Christchurch City Council rating
resolutions from 2004 to 2012, but I would also like to take the opportunity to wish the
council well. It is doing a great job in challenging times, and the people of Christchurch
appreciate it. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: I can see, Mr Deputy Speaker, that you
are allowing a very broad -ranging debate on this second reading of what is a very
narrow piece of legislation —a piece of legislation that is about validating rates in
Christchurch. I see that you are wanting us to traverse the terrain in all its many corners,
and I will, too, Mr Deputy Speaker—I will oblige. And I am sure my colleagues will, in
their contributions to this bill, feel free to frolic around the plains of Canterbury in how
they address this. Because as the speaker before me, the sponsor of this bill, said—and I
want to acknowledge the Hon Nicky Wagner —this is a very specific bill with a very
specific task: it is about rectifying a mistake that happened with the way rates were
struck in Christchurch over a period of time.
The Minister did say that it was a mistake made “with the best of intentions”. Well, I
am not sure whether mistakes can be made “with the best of intentions”. I do believe it
was probably a mistake made “without malevolence”. I do believe that it was probably a
mistake “not made on purpose”. But I do not really think that we can make mistakes
“with the best of intentions”. But none the less, Christchurch City Council finds itself in
the situation of having had a period of time when rates were not struck the way they
should have been. And the way that it has asked for this to be rectified is by a piece of
validating legislation. That is what we are here at the second reading to debate and to
kick around in a very broad-ranging way.
What we have here, though, is something that this Parliament should not be making a
habit of —that is, fixing mistakes via legislation. When we considered this piece of
legislation, we on the Local Government and Environment Committee were very much
of the united mind—if I could put it that way for our select committee—that actually—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Was Peter Dunne on it?

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: No, Peter Dunne was not on that committee and was not part
of the united mind. What we had was a crossing of the wa ys in wanting to ensure that
we as a Parliament are doing all that is in our power to ensure that we do not land back
here, having to fix up mistakes that have been made because we do not have adequate
1 Apr 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 2841
guidance or adequate oversight on how rates are struck by local body authorities. This is
something that I know, from my perspective on the committee, I am very keen to get on
the record.
During the first reading speeches on this bill, my colleague Su’a William Sio said
that this legislation is between a rock  and a hard place—that we know it has to be done,
that we need to fix this genuine error, but that it is never something we like doing. And
in the contribution he made on the bill, he said that he wanted to hear what it was that
the people of Christchurch had to say on the matter. The select committee, even before
this Parliament reconvened, was busy at work—the hard -working committee that we on
the Local Government and Environment Committee are. We were in Christchurch
hearing the submission—the one submission that we heard on this bill.
We did other work in Christchurch; I would not like to imply that we did not do a
full day’s work. We also had the question of the legislation that we debated in the
debate prior to this, the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill, to deal with on that day .
We heard from Christchurch City Council, and we heard how it was that it discovered
this error. The speaker before me, the Hon Nicky Wagner, described this —it really was
through the thorough order of their processes that it was discovered; that this transition
to a simpler language was found. I think it was very insightful. It was actually a really
good experience for the committee members to listen to that—and then to participate in
the discussion that followed about what the responsibilities of this House are , to ensure
that we do not get into those situations again.
Mr Deputy Speaker, you will notice that I have been speaking very specifically on
this very narrow piece of legislation, but now, since we are in the broad- ranging part of
the debate, I woul d like to venture out a little further, as it were, because what we did
hear the Minister do, after she dealt with the substance of why it is that we are here
today, was to put the legislation in the context of our recovery. Personally, I do not
think that this needs to be put in the context of our recovery; I think that, actually, to put
it so can be somewhat patronising to the people of Christchurch—that what we have is
something that other local authorities have gone through. But to use this debate to ta lk
about what a wonderful job it has been and about how great things are in Christchurch
is, actually, something I would rather not have seen. Yes, there are contentions around
how the recovery in Christchurch is going. I did not want to have to use this debate to
debate those issues, because that is not what this legislation is about —this is legislation
about how it is that Christchurch City Council is asking us to fix a genuine mistake. But
talking about organic food and nutraceuticals in the context of t his legislation, as we
heard from the previous speaker, is somewhat of a stretch.
I would like to talk about housing in the context of this bill, and, if we are going to
talk about the recovery, I want to talk about the lack of housing that we have in
Christchurch. I want to talk about the level of rates that people are paying in the city of
Christchurch—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Thank you. I would not like the m ember to think
that because the member promoting the bill made some magnanimous and inclusive
comments around Christchurch and its recovery that she should stray from her first
thoughts, which were that she should keep the debate relatively tight. She made  the
comment that she would not like to think that she had to stray broader than the mandate
of the bill, and I would remind her that she does not. In actual fact, the comments that
were made by the member initiating this legislation were magnanimous in re spect of
Christchurch, and were obviously well -meaning. I guess that what I am indicating to
this speaker and to other speakers who will take calls, is that they should bear in mind
the particular strain in which those comments were made, and bear in mind the scope of
this bill. If I was recalcitrant in some way by not paying as close attention as I should
2842 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 1 Apr 2015
have, that does not necessarily give subsequent speakers licence to wander off around
the paddock and cut their own track in respect of the scope of this  bill, which, as the
member has already conceded, is very narrow.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: Thank you, Mr Deputy Speaker. I take your wise words on
board. We are here tonight debating a ratings bill. Ratings are levelled on property, as
we all know—rates. And what we are validating here are mistakes that were made with
how the rates were struck in Christchurch on individual properties. Many of those
houses, actually, have now gone; some of the houses that this bill affects were actually
some of those that were demolished as a consequence of the red zone. I think we would
all acknowledge how sad that is and what Christchurch has been through, in terms of
that. But I would also note that perhaps we have not had the rebuilding of as many
houses as we would like to see, to replace those properties where rates could have been
struck, or otherwise had been struck. This is what we have to think about if we are
going to be thinking about this piece of legislation in the context of the rebuild and
recovery of Christchurch—what it means for our city; what it means for what we could
be. Because this is about the ratings base of Christchurch, this is about where people
live, and this is about the homes in which people enjoy their lives, when we are talking
about rates, because this is the way that it has been chosen to be done. So I would like to
raise that in the context of this legislation.
I think one of the things that some of the speakers said when this bill was previously
before this House did raise a question. I referred earlier to the contribution that my
colleague Su’a William Sio made, when he said that he invited members in
Christchurch—and I quote from William Sio’s speech: “We support this bill through its
first reading. I would invite all members and c itizens of Christchurch to take the
opportunity to submit on this bill and make their views known to this Government about
the lack of action that they are seeing in the rebuild there. Thank you.” That is from a
first reading speech on this bill.
I myself think it is a shame that we did not hear from more people and that we did
have only one submission on this bill. It would have been interesting to get feedback
from the people of Christchurch on this, but I guess one of the things that we know —
and I can reach across the House to my colleague Nicky Wagner, who is the sponsor of
this bill—is what the people of Christchurch have been through and just how tired many
of them are. There is a bit of fatigue, actually, among many people in Christchurch in
terms of input into consultative processes —because there have been a number of them.
There have many things for the people of Christchurch to have their say on and to input
into, and I think this is probably one of the reasons why we did not have as many
contributions as perhaps my colleague Su’a William Sio was thinking when he made
that comment in his first reading speech.
I think that we do stand here with a very narrow piece of legislation that does a very
specific task, which is about correcting a mistake that was made without malevolence. It
is a mistake that does need to be corrected, because we need our ratings to be struck in a
legal way and in accordance with the Local Government (Ratings) Act. Labour supports
this bill in the House. In no way is this any s lur on the Government, but we do not want
to be here again supporting more validating legislation, as I am sure my colleagues
across the House would concur. I think that we as a House need to turn our minds to
how it is that we can avoid being in this plac e again, whether that be through the audit
process or whether that be through issuing good guidance to councils as they strike their
rates, to ensure that resolutions that confer either the legality or illegality of rates and
how they are levied  are struck  and are something that we can have in place. Labour
supports this legislation. Thank you.
1 Apr 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 2843

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: As chairman of the Local
Government and Environment Committee, it gives me no pleasure at all this evening to
be standing in the Parliament of New Zealand supporting —reluctantly—retrospective
validating legislation for an albeit sincere and non -malicious mistake, but a mistake
none the less, made some 10 years ago by professional, highly paid, highly skilled,
competent-on-the-face-of-it people employed by the Christchurch City Council. This is
a bill that is sponsored by my colleague the Christchurch Central MP, the Hon Nicky
Wagner. She has set out very clearly in  her introductory comments to this second
reading the reasons why we are debating in Parliament tonight this piece of
retrospective validation legislation. The bill itself is promoted by the Christchurch City
Council, which was, of course, the author of the error. The bill validates specified rates
set between the 2004- 05 and the 2012- 13 financial years, and because of the rates
irregularities that came to light in the council’s review, the legislation is, frankly, the
only method for putting right an error  that occurred more than 10 years ago and well
before the Canterbury earthquakes.
Christchurch City Council failed to state in its rates resolution over those years that
the rates themselves were payable by instalment. The excuse, if you like, or the
rationale for the error was simply that it was to be a simple piece of internal local
legislation within the city council, something that councils do every year in terms of
providing for their fiscal responsibilities and their rating responsibilities under the Local
Government (Rating) Act 2002. But what happened in this case was that no resolution
was moved and passed through the council through the elected officials that ensured the
rates were to be payable by instalment. Furthermore, there was no date set by  which
those instalments would be paid, and further, there were no penalties set and no penalty
dates set for those instalments. Minister Wagner made the point in her comments —and
she is right—that, actually, no ratepayer has been negatively impacted as a result of this
error. But the simple matter is that had an alert ratepayer decided to challenge the city
council on these matters over any one of those 10 years, then court action would have
ensued and almost certainly the council would have come out the l oser from that
litigation. So that is a completely unsatisfactory situation for the ratepayers of
Christchurch, it is a completely unsatisfactory situation for the elected councillors of
Christchurch, and it is a completely unsatisfactory situation for the  highly paid and
professionally skilled employees who are supposed to oversee these relatively simple
matters.
The failures actually put the Christchurch City Council in breach of the Local
Government (Rating) Act 2002, and then, as a result of the invest igations in 2013, when
the irregularities were actually discovered, further irregularities were uncovered. They
were in respect of the council’s uniform annual general charge and some of the targeted
rates for the same period of time. Information about how  the liability for targeted rates
and the uniform annual general charge were to be calculated was simply not included in
the rates resolutions that were put to the council in the council chambers  for its
attention.
My colleague the Hon Nicky Wagner —correctly, I think—said that bad things
sometimes happen when you are trying to do good, but I would counter that by saying
that the road to hell is often paved with good intentions. Just because something is
meant to be simple, it does not mean that it needs to  be incomplete, it does not mean
that it needs to be inaccurate, and it does not mean that it needs to be incompetent. I
doubt that many, if any, of the officers responsible at the time—and I hasten to point out
that we are going back 10 years—would still be in the employ of the council, although I
am not 100 percent sure about that. Certainly, it is several chief executive officers ago.
So I am not necessarily going to pour scorn and derision upon current officers, but
2844 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 1 Apr 2015
council officers at the time failed the council, they failed the ratepayers, and they failed
themselves in terms of their professional ability and capability. Rates were calculated
correctly, rates were collected correctly, but the rates motion —the actual legal bit, the
piece that is importan t—was missed out, and that is a fundamental flaw for council
officers, who, actually, are employed to ensure that the i’s are dotted and the t’s are
crossed.
We had only one submission and, indeed, that was from the council itself. We
travelled to Christc hurch. As a select committee, we were able to link our visit with
some rather better legislative work, and that was to do with the Christchurch Arts
Centre and the bill that was discussed earlier this evening in Parliament. So when we
came to consider the Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill, we received
only one submission—one submission—from the council, and this is it. It is a mere two
pages. It is a relatively perfunctory submission. It contains a clinical analysis of what
happened, how it happened, and what needs to be done to correct it. The simple matter
is that what needs to be corrected is that this Parliament is required to pass retrospective
validating legislation to dig Christchurch City Council out of a hole. That is not a
process that this Parliament likes doing. It is not a process that I think any member of
the House thinks we should be spending too much time on. It is something that we
certainly do not expect from a council as large, as well -resourced, and as significant as
the Christchurch City Council.
What was immediately apparent to members of the select committee —and I think I
speak on behalf of most committee members —was that the submitters on behalf of the
council were relaxed almost to the point of being comatose in terms of their submission.
They seemed to be just appearing before us in a perfunctory manner, saying: “Oh well,
we made a mistake. All too bad, best endeavours, Parliament will put it right.” Well, I
am not sure that that is necessarily very good. In the 2- page submission from the
council there was no comment about contrition. There was no concession as to liability.
There was no attempt to identify those people who were responsible. There was no
indication that any kind of employment disciplinary action had been taken. In fact, there
was no sense at all of any sense of personal responsibility for the situation that the
council found itself in—which Parliament now finds itself having to remedy.
So it is fair to say that I thought, as chair, that our committee w as singularly
underwhelmed by the submission of the Christchurch City Council, and I for one did
not come away from hearing its oral submission or indeed reading its written
submission with any sense of renewed confidence in the future prospects for getting
things right. That may be a little bit harsh, but I think that as a Parliament we could
reasonably and sensibly expect a higher level of professionalism from one of the
country’s largest councils. To expect anything less is an abrogation of its role and
responsibility as a significant and large council but also in terms of the roles of
professionals and employees of the council.
We all live and work in an environment of constant change. We are all only human
and we all make mistakes, but this was a mista ke of quite significant proportions. The
fact that it did not negatively impact on ratepayers is a matter more of good luck than
good management. I very reluctantly commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: Firstly, I just want to make
some general comments about the Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill
and look to some of the substance of it. Then I want to make some comments with
regard to what the member on the other side of the House, Scott Simpson, has just said.
I think that by the end of this particular session we will be intimately aware of each
individual part of this bill. It is a small bill; it is a fix -up bill. There is no denying that. It
1 Apr 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 2845
has been well traversed that the council needs this bill to pass in order to correct an
issue that developed out of some work about 10 years ago.
When you look at the bill you see that the preamble to the bill is longer than the rest
of the bill. It is interesting; there are a couple of sections, two parts, to fix up the issue
around the fact that we need to ensure we can validate the payment dates for the rates
and validate the penalties on those unpaid rates. We can look at the setting of the r ates,
that the revenue can actually lawfully be received by the council, and that it can recover
the penalties on any outstanding rates. That is in Part 1 of this bill. Clause 4 looks
specifically at the rates for the Church Bay sewer loan, the Church Bay water loan, the
Governors Bay sewer loan, and the Governors Bay water loan. There are definitions
around rates, rates invoices, the specific components within the rates —for example, the
water fire service connection  rate—and waste minimisation. But they ar e for the
specific periods mentioned previously —the 2004- 05 years and latterly the 2012- 13
years. If we do not fix this, if we do not pass this legislation, it means that the
Christchurch City Council will continue to be in breach of section 24 of the Loca l
Government (Rating) Act 2002.
Thank you to the Local Government and Environment Committee for going to
Christchurch to hear the submissions on this bill and on the previous bill concerning the
Arts Centre. There was one submitter on this bill. Obviously, it was the council, and the
bill came back to the House largely unchanged.
The previous speaker talked about how relaxed the officials were in their submission.
He talked about the lack of contrition the council officials demonstrated and the
disregard they had for their roles and their jobs by allowing this error to occur in the
first place. I have to defend the officials of Christchurch City Council. It is a difficult
job, but it is also rather ironic that that member chose to place upon the officials t hat
responsibility when in this House every year we are presented with legislation that fixes
up mistakes we have made in the past. Everyone makes mistakes. This is a bill that fixes
up an error, and I do think it is ironic that in the privilege of this House we can condemn
the officials from the Christchurch City Council but we do not take responsibility for
errors we make in the drafting of legislation we pass. I want Mr Simpson to just
recognise that these are hard -working people, and we are currently ex periencing in our
council in Christchurch City an extraordinary amount of work. They are currently
engaged in the long -term plan process. There is a lot of stuff going on in Christchurch,
and I, for one, am supporting the fact that our officials work very hard. They cannot be
here to defend themselves today.
This bill is about the relationship between the council and central government. I have
to say I am not entirely sure that the relationship that this Government has with the
Christchurch City Council ha s been all that helpful or robust in recent times. Again, I
say I do defend the officials of Christchurch City Council. They are doing their job.
They have admitted they have found a mistake and it is our job now to correct that
mistake, and we should do s o with good heart and good intent. I do not think there is
much more I can say on the bill.

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: There is.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: Oh, is there? OK; I shall say a little bit more. [ Interruption] I
have been given the instructions. I want to just comment on that relationship between
central government and the Christchurch City Council, because it is very important that
we do what we can to ensure that relationship is strong. There have been issues —and I
speak from my ow n electorate—between what the expectations of ratepayers and
taxpayers are, and where the relationship between the council and central government
has not entirely been that consistent or coherent.
2846 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 1 Apr 2015
I want to talk about the infrastructure that we are still w aiting for in Christchurch
East.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: Pity the councillors.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: That is right. Thank you, Mr Nash. We should all be defending
councillors. It is a tough job.
We are currently looking at ensuring that the infrastructure, particularly the
horizontal infrastructure, in Christchurch East, is remediated to a point where we can
actually have smooth roads, like other parts of our city. But I have to say that in that
regard I do not know that the Government has actually come to the party for our
ratepayers in Christchurch East. There is a partnership that needs to be forged and needs
to continue to be robust. However, I am concerned that that is not the case and that we
are still subject to some very damaged roads, some very dusty, dusty outlooks . We are
still replacing the sewer and the rest of the lines in Christchurch East when much of the
rest of the city is 100 percent back to normal.
I want to conclude now. I think I have pretty much said what I need to say on the
matter. We do support this bill and commend it to the House. Thank you.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I call the member for Bay of Plenty, Todd Muller.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: It is “Muller”, Mr Deputy Speaker, if
it is possible to just anglicise it. It would have been “Mueller” back in 1860 when our
family arrived, but it is now “Muller”.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Surname validation.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: Yes, thank you for that contribution. I am rising to speak
similarly reluctantly, really, to the Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill. I
acknowledge your ongoing interest in this topic,  Mr Deputy Speaker, and also that of
the many thousands of people in Christchurch who will be sitting on the edge of their
seats waiting for this piece of legislation to finally get through here this evening. I do
want to acknowledge the Hon Nicky Wagner.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: They’ll be asleep if they listen to this speech.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: I will amp it up shortly; we just want to start slow. So, well done
for your contribution, Nicky Wagner. It is obviously something that needs to be done
and I thought you articulated the rationale for that very well. I also acknowledge, again,
Scott Simpson for his leadership of the Local Government and Environment Committee
and the way we have managed this issue through as a group.
As I am sure we all kn ow, the bill that is in front of us this evening is the
Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill. Its purpose is to correct an
administrative anomaly. Unfortunately, there is clear precedent for this. We have been
here before. Maybe this is a Sout h Island thing, I do not know, but we were here a year
or so ago for the Tasman District Council (Validation and Recovery of Certain Rates)
Bill. That obviously was passed to fix some retrospective administrative errors. I
guess—if we are to be very genero us in our outlook—we could say that local
government is particularly complex. We have 67 territorial authorities, 12 city councils,
53 district councils; six territorial authorities —Auckland Council, the Chatham Islands
Council, Nelson, Gisborne, Tasman, a nd Marlborough— are unitary authorities, and I
guess with all of this complexity there is going to be the occasional error. I guess one
argument—and we have heard it particularly from the other side so far this evening —is
that, you know, this happens infrequently, human errors can occur, and when they do it
is appropriate for us to get together and fix them, which is what we are doing this
evening.
Essentially, the assistance that we are collectively offering tonight is because the
council failed in its rat es resolution to state that the rates were payable by instalments,
what the payment dates were for those instalments, and what penalties would be added
1 Apr 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 2847
for late payment in these and previous years. The administrative breach, to be technical
for a moment with respect to the bill, is a breach to the Local Government (Rating) Act
2002, mostly around section 44, “Notice of rates assessment”, and section 45, “Contents
of rates assessment”. The relevant part here, for those in the House who are particularly
interested in this detail, is section 44, “Notice of rates assessment—(1) A local authority
must deliver a rates assessment to a ratepayer to give notice of the ratepayer’s liability
for rates on a rating unit. (2) A ratepayer is liable for rates on a rating unit when the
local authority delivers the rates assessment for that unit to the ratepayer.” So that is
section 44—[Interruption]—for a moment there I thought I was going to get a point of
order that might have stopped me.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: That would have required me to have been listening.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: You are following this and enjoying it, no doubt. In section 45,
“Contents of rates assessment”, the particular part here that caught Christchurch city
was “(m) the methods by whic h rates may be paid and the date or, if the rates are
payable by instalments, the dates by which specified amounts must be paid: (n) if
applicable,—(i) the penalty regime of the local authority; and (ii) a warning that, if rates
are not paid on time, a pen alty may be added under that regime:”. So, as you can see,
this is a complex process. The city council in many respects, as we have heard this
evening, was trying to simplify that, but in its enthusiasm to make the rates setting
process more easy for its constituents to understand it missed a pretty critical part in that
process.
I did a rough count on the amount of ratepayers in New Zealand. There are roughly 2
million. If each ratepayer receives a quarterly rates assessment, that is about 8 million
rates transactions that occur. So I guess, again, to be charitable, if you look at this
particular error in the context of New Zealand as a whole, it is not extraordinary that we
have to be here tonight. I do have a lot of sympathy with the sentiment that our
chairman, Scott Simpson, has articulated this evening on two points. Firstly, we do
expect that officers of councils are familiar with a ratings Act that came in in 2002 and
would have the appropriate internal controls to ensure that they are following the correct
process accordingly. Secondly, when an error has been found and you are asking
Parliament to make a change to validate you and to essentially get you off a hook, you
would expect some degree of contriteness, and I think Scott, the member for
Coromandel, summarised that very well. I was, like him, very disappointed that there
was not a sense of acknowledgment that Christchurch City Council had to put the
Parliament through a process when, quite frankly, our collective wisdom could be well
focused on things other than this. I was disappointed that when we flew down to meet
with the council there was a degree of offhandedness in respect of the way it was
approaching this particular issue.
What you would also expect in this debate —and I am sure we are go ing to hear it
shortly with my good friend and colleague Mr Mark—is a reference to the role of
auditors. I just thought I might get in first here because I have heard him speak very
eloquently on this before —perhaps because of his passion for local governm ent—
saying that somehow if the governors and officers of a particular local council slip up,
then really it should be the auditors who pick it up, and really it is the auditors who
should be hung out to dry. Of course, they are a key part of it, but I do hope that the
governors of a particular council and the officers of a particular council do not take the
approach that actually they can do the best they can but it is really the job of an external
auditor to pick up the things they miss. That is not what best practice is. It is nowhere
near best practice. There should be a strong internal audit function. There should be a
good mix of governors and officers participating in that internal audit process and they
should have the capacity, capability, and focus to ensure that they pick up these errors,
2848 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 1 Apr 2015
and not have an approach that says that if they miss something, an auditor should cover
it for them.
In that regard it was very positive to see that the Society of Local Government
Managers has identified that the re is room for improvement. We saw that in the report
back from the department and the various work that is under way to improve councils’
practices with respect to setting rates resolutions. I was very pleased —and I am sure the
various members of the sele ct committee were very pleased —to see that work under
way, not before time. We have an expectation that the officers of councils are at the
very best level of best practice and process. We really should not be in this position
again of having to cover up f or administrative anomalies. With that, I would like to add
my somewhat reluctant voice on this side of the House to this particular bill, the
Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill, and will remain very interested in the
ongoing debate as it occurs over the next hour. Thank you.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: Like others in this House, I rise reluctantly to speak on
the Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill. The average daily cost of running
this Parliament is over half a million dollars and the average bill costs $1.43 million,
according to the Parliamentary Library. So this local bill, promoted by the Christchurch
City Council, is a very expensive way of fixing errors that the city counci l could have
avoided.
As others have noted, the council breached the Local Government (Rating) Act 2002.
It made mistakes in the way it worded its rates resolutions in relation to the payment
dates for rates, the authority to impose penalties on unpaid ra tes, and the targeted rates
for Church Bay and Governors Bay. The council was certainly trying to simplify the
resolutions, but these mistakes continued for 10 years. Although the bill attracted only
one submission, even though it is retrospective legislation, it is probably uncontroversial
because ratepayers do not engage with the minutiae of rates resolutions and because the
actual rating demands that the council sent out were correctly worded.
So the council has made mistakes, and I share with other mem bers the concerns
about the offhand way in which its officers presented to the select committee , but the
city council in its long -term plan for 2015- 25 is proposing to make an even bigger
mistake than the ones that this bill aims to correct. In that long -term plan, the council is
proposing to sell off or sell down shares in strategic a ssets like Orion New Zealand, the
Lyttelton Port Co ., Christchurch International Airport , Cit y Care, EcoCare, and Red
Bus. The dividends from these council -owned companies through Christchurch City
Holdings have provided a key source of revenue to Christchurch. They have  helped
fund the council’s services and its activities, and they have helped to offset rates.
Rates in Christchurch have been lower than in Selwyn and Waimakariri, which are
neighbouring councils. They have been lower than in other city centres like Hamil ton,
Wellington, and Tauranga . The cash dividend that the city council will get from these
companies in the forthcoming financial year is estimated to be around $46 million. That
has the effect of lowering council rates by 13 percent. Those cash dividends have
averaged 3 percent in the last 3 years and 4 percent in the last 10 years, and there has
been a 26 percent return to shareholders since 1996 because of asset growth and
appreciation in capital value. That has been a very good return to the people of
Christchurch. If the council proceeds to sell off those assets, the dividends stream will
halve.
So it is a very short -sighted decision, which the council is being panicked into
making because of the National Government’s reluctance to renegotiate the cost-sharing
agreement with the council. It is reluctant to take costly projects like the stadium out of
the cost -sharing agreement —off the council’s books —and it is reluctant to re -engage
1 Apr 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 2849
and contribute a fairer share to the costs of repairing the council’s horizontal
infrastructure.
The council has come to Parliament to ask us to fi x these problems with its rates
resolutions—to, effectively, validate the payment dates for the rates and the issues
around penalties. It has come to Parliament to ensure that all the money that it has
received from the rates that it has levied is lawful, so  that it can lawfully go after people
who have not paid rates and not face a legal challenge there, but it will not be able to
come back to Parliament and ask the House to solve the problems that the sell- off of
these strategic assets like Orion, like the port company , and like the airport company
will cause. They are problems where ratepayers in the future will be complaining about
the rise in their rates because the revenue base for the council has narrowed. It will have
to rely much more on rates rather than dividend income, and we will not be able to fix
those problems.
The council should be looking at alternatives to asset sales to meet the financial
shortfall. It should take  a much more rigorous look at its own spending and it should
scale back some of the roading projects. It should renegotiate the cost -sharing
agreement. We need a much wider revenue base, not a narrower one. I could go on and
talk at some length about the p roblems with mixed -ownership models, but I do not
think, Mr Deputy Speaker, you would be comfortable with that.
So coming back to the bill, I was puzzled that the Society of Local Government
Managers, the Department of Internal Affairs, and Local Governme nt New Zealand
have not done more to improve council practice around rates resolutions, because , as
Todd Muller mentioned, this is the third piece of legislation we have had to deal with in
recent years where we have had to validate council rates -setting procedures. Belatedly,
work has been done to improve practice. There have been seminars conducted. The
Society of Local Government Managers is updating and expanding its guide on rates
setting. There has been a guide for elective members, which is being set  out and
developed. But this problem is nothing compared with the problems that will arise if the
city council is bullied by Government into selling Christchurch assets. We will be
supporting this bill, but we do so reluctantly. Thank you.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: It is with a degree of mixed feelings that I rise to speak to
this bill on behalf of New Zealand First, and to indicate that New Zealand First will
reluctantly—very reluctantly—support this piece of legis lation. I said earlier on today
that the difficulty of speaking at about the No. 7 slot is that pretty much that all the
things you really need to talk about have already been said, and I do not want to bore
the House by going through all of the detail and minutiae again. However, that said,
there are some things that do need to be said.
We have already heard in the blow -by-blow accounts of respective members of the
Local Government and Environment Committee as to the circumstances that brought
about this piece of legislation and that brought it to the House. The fact that we are
passing retrospective legislation in this House does not sit well with New Zealand First
at all—at all. That is a bad precedent. It is something that should not be visited in this
House, and the fact that we are doing it for a third time, as has been mentioned, is an
indictment on those people who are responsible. I am not going to be so forgiving, in
my speech, of some of the things that have led us to this point.
The submission from the Christchurch City Council makes interesting reading, as
does the Department of Internal Affairs report to the select committee. There were some
questions that were asked by the select committee before I was back in the House in
November. It is interesting going through and reading the answers, specifically when
the select committee back on 27 November 2014 asked this of the department: “The
committee requested copies of Christchurch City Council’s audit reports for each of the
2850 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 1 Apr 2015
financial years involved. The committee also asked for information [ as to ] who
undertook the audits each year; the cost of the  audits; whether the audit reports raised
any issues with the rates resolutions ; and the name of the Christchurch City Council’s
Chief Executive at the relevant times.”
It is astonishing when you look at some things. Having been a M ayor of Carterton, I
am finding it really quite —I am going to try not to be smug, and I will try desperately,
because that is not a good characteristic and we have been  seeing too much of that in
this House, right up until last weekend. Some of the smugness  has been knocked off
some faces, but I am going to try not to be smug. But I have heard consistently how
super-cities are the be- all and end- all—how economies of scale solve all manner of
problems. I have heard so much claptrap out of the mouth of Fran Wi lde and the Local
Government Commission toadies—and I will call them toadies because that is all I see
them as —who said things like you will get the high level of expertise in local
government that is required for the future only if you amalgamate all the councils into
one. So let us look at this super-city in the south.
This super -city in the south has managed to do something that Carterton District
Council, the third- smallest council in New Zealand, has never done. I know from my
experience that if you have a competent chief executive officer and competent staff
when you are passing the resolutions for your annual plan—in which you lay out the
rates, the uniform annual general charges, the targeted rates, and the rates increases —
your run sheet tells you, as the mayor, precisely what resolutions you must be passing.
Your chief executive officer and his financial manager will lay down very clearly and
specifically the requirements of the Act, and those resolutions will be passed and they
will be put on to paper, into words, prior to the rates bills going out and prior to the
annual plan being finally endorsed and published. Without that being done, the annual
report does not get approved.
Yet here is a super -city with all of the power that it can muster to be able to hire the
best—and who were the best? Well, going into this report from the Ministry of Internal
Affairs, we now know that the mayors were Mayor Moore, Mayor Parker —
unfortunately, the Hon Lianne Dalziel  came in right at the tail end and has to cl ean up
the mess. But we also have chief executive officers Dr Lesley McTurk and —get this;
this is the high level of competence that a super-city delivers—Tony Marryatt.
So who is the chief executive officer who oversaw the bulk of these stuff -ups? Well,
it was one Mr Tony Marryatt, who became famous down in Christchurch for racking up
Hooters bills when on the Christchurch City Council. It was one Mr Tony Marryatt,
who got an $800,000 payout—I am pretty sure it was about that . Looking at Wikipedia,
it talks about an $800,000 payout. Mr Tony Marryatt was the chief executive officer at
Hamilton who got totally offside with the mayor and the council of Hamilton, and was
one of the people responsible for the massive loss that the V8  Supercars races made. It
was Mr Tony Marryatt, who caused a high level of anxiety amongst people in
Christchurch that resulted in demonstrations and protests with about 4,000 people
turning up because he got a $70,000 pay rise. Stop press! Tony Marriott got a $70,000
pay rise as the chief executive officer at the very time he was stuffing up.
Well, I do not want to hear anybody talk to me and my people, the good people of
the Wairarapa—least of all the MP for the Wairarapa, who thinks that super -cities are
going to bring economies of  scale and sharper people into the management —when this
is the sort of thing one gets. Carterton has never had to face this. Carterton has never
had to come cap in hand to Parliament asking that it validate its rates bills over how
